[h2]Shadow of the Tomb Raider: Definitive Edition Review[/h2]

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
We all know & love Lara Croft. Square Enix couldn’t have made a better ending to the Tomb Raider Trilogy than this. The transformation of Lara Croft from the prey to the predator is what we all waited for, and this game finally gives us our long-yearned desire. Can Lara master the deadly jungle & overcome terrifying tombs to save the world from the apocalypse she started?
 
 [h1]About Lara Croft….I mean the game[/h1]
 
[h3][u][b]Storyline[/b][/u][/h3]
 
 The story picks off from where Rise of The Tomb Raider stopped. Compared to the inexperienced Lara from the previous two parts, here, she is well aware of all her abilities and also knows what to do against the Trinity. As always, Lara is accompanied by her best friend, Jonah, who Lara relies on a lot. It’s not clearly visible, but the story could have not been set in motion without Jonah’s help as he helps Lara take major decisions & find clues. I, obviously, do not want to spoil this well-woven story, hence I will not be revealing anything. I Will just give a really short intro:
 
 [i] As the game unfolds, Lara Croft seeks the key for a Silver Box with positive intentions to help the people but ends up releasing a catastrophic apocalypse, endangering thousands of lives. The story revolves around how she will fix her mistakes and the obstacles (Mainly Trinity) that fall onto her path. [/i]
 
 The previous games had at least a bit of Open-World Freedom during main quests, but this game makes you take the pre-defined route. They encouraged the use of curiosity, to bring out one of Lara’s main characteristics to the player. Using curiosity permits you to enjoy this game & discover hidden tomb/treasures etc. 
 
  Funnily enough, we don’t have freedom in combat too. The game wants you to take a Stealthier Approach rather than a direct assault as you could in the previous parts of this trilogy. For instance, in one part, the only weapon you have is a knife/Pickaxe and the enemies have legit Assault Rifle & Armor, so a sane person would obviously take the Stealth approach as there is no chance of survival otherwise. 
 
 [h3][b][u]Gameplay [/u][/b][/h3]
 
 The game has the classic Tomb Raider mechanics along with newly introduced mechanics that shows Lara is now experienced. You can now Rappel down from higher spots instead of Jumping down or falling. You can also throw your Axe to reach places that are out of your reach. They made it so you can overhang over ledges & ceilings. They increased the Swimming mechanics as there are several instances where she’s thrown underwater & survive while hiding from dangerous creatures like Piranhas, holding her breath & finding a way out. 
 
 Combat has been altered to encourage Stealth. You can cover yourself in mud and hide behind vines on walls. You can jump on tree branches and drop jump on enemies, executing them. Or use your bow, shoot an arrow with a rope attached to it, pull in the enemy & hang them on the branch, then choke them to death. There are so many ways to get stealth kills. Combat is overall smooth & decent. But I prefer the freedom granted in the previous games. 
 
 Like several other RPGish type games, SOTR also has a skill tree. There are three paths you can follow; 
 [list]
 [*] Seeker (Perception)
 [*] Scavenger (Handicraft)
 [*] Warrior (Physical Capabilities)
 [/list]
 
 These can be unlocked by earning skill points. The easiest way to obtain these is to just follow the main story. The other side quests, tombs, etc. give you rewards but, in my opinion, they are kinda useless as you can sustain the main story with the items you get. I feel like they are just there so the player gets more content for the high price of the game. 
 
 You can upgrade your weapons too. Firearms play a vital role in survival. Personally, I prefer using the bow as it’s One-Shot One-Kill to enemies with no armor & is silent. You can also use Fire Arrows, Exploding Arrows, or Fear Arrows, which make this weapon even better. I personally had a lot of fun using fear arrows to make the enemies turn against their comrades, might sound sadistic but was needed for Survival. I forgot to mention that you can change outfits. Certain outfits give the player some buffs. But if you want Lara to look hot, you need to sacrifice the buffs. I used the fitness outfit as she looked o.o in it. 
 
 You can hunt for animals to get supplies to upgrade your items & crafting. Hunting has been brought up a notch as now animals flee when they even sense you a bit. But ofc, hunting with an Assault Rifle is a piece of cake. 
 
 [h3][b][u] Graphics & Audio [/u][/b][/h3]
 
 Graphically, all the games that are part of the trilogy were beautiful. But Shadow of the Tomb Raider is even more beautiful. From tombs to Caverns, the size of everything was increased, offering more areas to explore & permitting Lara to use her abilities pretty well. Everything is detailed to perfection for the best visual experience. From the high rising mountains to the splashing waterfalls, everything was a real feast for the eyes. You see green everywhere, a very calming color! The one thing in this game that obliviously steals the limelight is Lara herself. She looks stunning as always! Well, there’s nothing much to speak on the aural aspect of the game as the dialogue deliveries were on point. I liked how they had an option where you can choose to permit the NPCs to speak in their native languages for a more realistic experience. This is the first time I came across such an option!

[h1] Pros [/h1]
 [list]
 [*] Purely a Story-driven game.
 [*] Beautiful Graphics. Lara Croft is a feast to the eyes as always. 
 [*] Loads of Side-missions & Tombs to complete.
 [*] Skill tree that allows you to make Lara even stronger.
 [*] Upgradable weapons. There’s a lot of secondary fire modes to the weapons. The different types of arrows available for use make the bow stand out from the rest of the weapons. 
 [*] Jonah never leaves your side. Yes, this is a Pro as Jonah is the best of the best when it comes to friends. 
 [*] Your sense of curiosity drives the gameplay by helping you find hidden objects/tombs. 
 [*] You can choose different difficulties for different aspects of the games. The aspects are: Puzzles, Combat & Environmental Exploration. There are four levels of difficulty; Easy, normal, hard & deadly obsession.
 [/list]
 
 [h1] Cons [/h1]
 [list]
 [*] The main story is really short. I finished it in under 10 hours. 
 [*] Side quests and tombs are quite unnecessary when it comes to progress towards the Main Story. It feels like they just squeezed it in there for content.
 [/list]
 
 [h1] The Finale [/h1]
 
 I am a big fan of the Tomb Raider trilogy. I enjoyed each & every one of the games. They have something in them that makes me hooked to them. Well, I am sure it’s Lara Croft but okay. Jokes aside, this is a real masterpiece and if you don’t play it, you are missing something wonderful. But yeah, the game comes with a heavy price tag for a few hours of fun. I recommend getting it on a very good sale.

Ratings:9.5/10

Well, here I am, just finished the game.

I'll be honest with you, I was really looking forward to this game, and whilst I did most certainly enjoy it, im still disappointed. Im going to start this review with the negatives, and end on a more happy note.

Though the game length isn't short, took me about 20 hours to complete around 75%, it still feels a lot shorter than Rise of the Tomb Raider. I can't really explain why, but I found myself quite suprised as to how fast the story was progressing.

Speaking of the story, I hate to say it, but it's really quite bad. All the characters are pretty much bland and without any character or personality (with the exception of Lara and Jonah). I guarantee you you won't care about anyone else. Also the story just really lacks depth, I didnt get invested in it, at any point.

Then we get to another really weird issue. The dialogue. Whilst the quality of the audio is excellent, I can't help but notice quest givers pause a lot longer inbetween sentences than what I would declare a normal way of speaking. It get's really bad when you are sitting at camp when Lara is narrating, sometimes she pauses like 5 seconds before saying anything. Literally half the time I think shes done talking and then suddenly theres more. It's just weird and feels unnatural.

Then we get to the gameplay, first of all, I find there to be a lack of enemies. Sure you do fight quite regularly, whether it's stealth or combat, but, I just ended the game feeling like I hadn't really done much in the way of combat. [spoiler]
In the trailers you see this cool scene in a dark jungle where Lara is taking out some soldiers, whilst this is in the game, its literally one quick sequence where you have no weapons, just a knife. There is stealth in the rest of the game of course, but I was hoping there were more areas like the one I just mentioned, instead of one litte sequence. [/spoiler]

Then we get to the "hubs". Do you feel like talking to everyone? I most certainly didn't because of the bad story, so good luck with that. I literally walked past most random civilian dialogue people simply muttering the phrase "I dont give a sh*t". Sure it gives you information about secrets and possible tomb locations, but as I said, I just didnt care.

Then theres another issue: You will be locked from selecting certain outfits and using certain weapons for a big portion of the game. Now don't get me wrong, I understand the reasoning behind this, it's to "blend in", but I just found it really , really annoying. 

To end on a more positive note:
The tombs are excellent.
The new climbing mechanics work well
The graphics are amazing.
Excellent voice acting for Lara and Jonah
Stealth is just as good as it was, though really easy due to bad AI.

To sum up, if you liked Rise of the Tomb Raider, you will like this, BUT, you will feel it is inferior.

I do recommend this game, but I would wait for a sale, especially if you loved Rise of the Tomb Raider.

Seeing as though this is the last game in the trilogy, I do want it said that I really do hope they make more of these games, they are a joy to play.

Shadow of the Tomb Raider is the third game in the franchise’s modern era, and continues the Trinity storyline established in Tomb Raider (2013) and Rise of the Tomb Raider. Everyone’s favourite English archaeologist, Lara Croft, must locate a powerful artefact that is hidden somewhere in South America, before Trinity can use it for their own agenda.

The Good

•	The environment is gorgeous, featuring dense jungles, waterfalls, lakes, ancient villages, dark caves, and massive tombs containing some lethal traps. There’s more underwater exploration than previous games, which is something I definitely approve of. [Spoiler]There’s also an interesting flashback to Croft manor.[/spoiler]
•	My favourite aspect of Tomb Raider games is the puzzle solving, so I’m pleased that Shadow’s gameplay involves a nice balance of combat and puzzles. The optional challenge tombs in particular contain some massive ancient mechanisms, which felt really satisfying to solve. My favourite puzzles in the older Tomb Raider games involved raising and lowering the water level, and Shadow features a couple of good water puzzles.
•	Combat is enjoyable. Along her journey Lara will have to face Trinity soldiers, aggressive wildlife, and something else that I won’t spoil. There’s a greater emphasis on stealth kills. Lara still has the bow for getting silent headshots, but you can also cover her in mud and hide against walls like Arnold in Predator, hide in long grass, climb trees, and perform takedowns from underwater. When its time to go loud, you can use an assault rifle, shotgun, pistol, molotovs, and poison arrows which confuse enemies and make them attack their friends. Aiming weapons with a mouse feels responsive.
•	You can separately adjust the difficulty of combat, puzzles and exploration, although I played with all set to hard, and honestly I think most players will cope just fine with this. I especially liked the ability to turn off puzzle solving hints, and the white paint that shows you where to jump next, so that I could work out what to do myself without the game getting impatient and giving me the answer.
•	Voice acting is mostly good, including another excellent performance from Camilla Luddington as Lara.
•	It took me 24 hours to finish the story and all challenge tombs and side quests.
•	I was able to easily maintain 60 FPS and controls are fully rebindable. I’ve had a couple of crashes when exiting the game, but no problems during actual gameplay.
•	There’s an option to just hold a button during QTEs instead of mashing repeatedly. (I mean, I’d prefer no QTEs at all, but at least this is a small improvement).
•	This game is approximately 1000% more enjoyable than the Tomb Raider film that came out earlier this year, where Hollywood proved they still don’t understand videogame characters.

The Bad

•	The story is a bit disappointing, and definitely doesn’t match the quality of the previous two games. The promise created by an intense opening just seems to fizzle out, especially in the second half. Its been said that a story is only as strong as its villain, and Shadow’s primary antagonist, the leader of Trinity, is just kinda boring.
•	The game seems to be in a permanent tutorial mode, frequently displaying messages about how to perform actions that you’ve already done dozens of times. For example, you’ll be running along the edge of a cliff, admiring the scenery, the lake below and the jungle in the distance, when suddenly you’ll see some floating text telling you how to do a swan dive for the 15th time. There’s no option to disable these messages, and I saw them all the way to the end of the game. Its immersion breaking, it spoils the mood, and it really needs to be patched.
•	You can’t toggle walk when using mouse/keyboard. Default movement speed is run, and you have to hold a button to walk. Walking is important when exploring narrow ledges and avoiding traps in dark caves. I ended up binding walk to a mouse thumb button which seemed like the most natural feeling button to hold in for lengthy periods of time, but it wasn’t ideal. You can toggle both sprint and aim down sights, so why no walk toggle? Again, this really should be patched.

The Recommendation

Shadow of the Tomb Raider has enjoyable puzzle solving and combat, but is let down slightly by a disappointing story. If you’re a fan of the franchise you should definitely buy it, but perhaps not at full price. If you’ve never played Tomb Raider before, I’d recommend playing Tomb Raider (2013) and Rise of the Tomb Raider first. (Tomb Raider Anniversary is still my favourite, so you should check that out too).

[b][u][h1] MY REVIEW OF THE SHADOW OF THE TOMB RAIDER GAME [/h1][/u][/b]
[b][h1] In South America [/h1][/b]
[b][i] The most significant difference that always characterised each Tomb Raider episode: the change of location. My preference is with the colder climate (this also means that this episode omits the Endurance mode) but it is always nice to see how a new location can affect gameplay. Areas with battle now allow Lara to go back into hiding by bathing in mud. An interesting concept - I particularly liked how she could move along the wall out of plain sight due to the overgrown flora. [/i][/b]
[b][i] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0NN7UCIAHsQ&t=17s [/i][/b]
[b][h1] Trinity [/h1][/b]
[b][i] The bad guys return and Lara now encounters a leader called Pedro Dominguez. It is nice to add a face to Trinity this time and Pedro actually knows more of Lara than she thinks. Cutscenes are amazing with the usual high-quality voice acting on everybody's part and there is increased focus on Lara's childhood and father this time. There are a couple of twists here an there - as usual later on a new form of enemy appears to make the story more exciting. This alone does not make the plot totally different so the creators decided to include more peril by choosing artifacts with great power. Let's just say that Lara's race against Trinity has time factored in. [/i][/b]
[b][i] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VwljTbmEjvw&t=4s [/i][/b]
[b][h1] Gameplay [/h1][/b]
[b][i] You know how the developers add new elements even when it is not necessary. Gameplay in the previous two instalments was fast and dynamic enough. Still, there's new gear, of course. Overhang climbing is now possible with the use of special boots. I think this feature was unnecessary and thank god no puzzles were based on this. Grappling down from cliffs, however, is a nice new addition. 

We find all sorts of materials - beside upgrading our weapons we can craft pieces of clothing. Upper and lower body pieces are available but we can also acquire full body outfits. These add bonuses so getting dressed before a fight we can decide if we intend to aim for a more stealthy approach or go full guns blazing by putting on something that gives Lara health regeneration. And, naturally, we can give Lara the "old" look by applying skins from previous games (this is a purely cosmetic choice here).

Other than these small changes or additional stuff gameplay mechanics remain the same. I liked the inclusion of air pockets during underwater sequences which made it possible to increase the time spent in such areas. Once again Lara can decipher various monuments (her language skills increase gradually) and there are tons of relics and letters to be found out there. You'll return to previous locations by using the camp system several times just to get that 100% completion.

Graphics appear to be enhanced once again; I cannot comment on the latest RTX technology but everything else looked stunning as usual. Two more small adjustments done to walkthroughs: there are difficulty settings we can choose from but they are broken down into various elements we can adjust separately. Additionally, there is a possibility to make immersion better by allowing the NPCs to use their native language instead of English. [/i][/b]

[b][h1] Longevity [/h1][/b]
[b][i] What else to say about Shadow of Tomb Raider? Another great entry in the series where there are more and much bigger tombs. The DLCs also focus on these extra challenges. The hub area we visit appears to be greater and there are many side missions to complete. It's worth investing time into these as getting the rewards will make Lara stronger. There is a New Game+ mode available with additional skills we can purchase only during this second walkthrough. [/i][/b]
[b][i] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tdEfROL2Wx8&t=340s [/i][/b]
[b][i] I had fun with the latest instalment. The puzzles were sometimes annoying (oh boy the one in the church was just awful!) but gave me a good challenge, nonetheless. Of all 3 episodes this one has the most interesting story and definitely the most satisfying end game boss battle. [/i][/b]

[h1] The story? Wack. The dialogue? Wack. The characters? Wack. Exploration? Tight as fucc. [/h1]

It seems like the developers didn’t exactly know what they wanted Lara Croft to be, and so she struggles to find an identity that is believable and makes sense. Lara oscillates between being an emotional, gentle, cutesy, light-hearted goody-two-shoes on the one hand, and a battle-hardened, dispassionate, cold-blooded murderer on the other hand.

Within the first 30 minutes, it’s basically established that you are a mass killer responsible for the deaths of thousands of civilians, without much of an emotional reaction from Lara apart from an indifferent “oops”. Weird flex, but ok. As soon as you engage with civilians one on one, however, you are the sweetest, most compassionate puritan imaginable, incapable of hurting a fly. [i]Bi_tch, you just killed north of a thousand people, and will kill another thousand in combat throughout the game.[/i] The juxtaposition stretches suspension of disbelief way beyond its breaking point.

Also strange: you only ever kill men. Where’s the female representation? Don't these men have family, hopes, dreams and fears as much as Lara does? The narrative of brave, oppressed female leaders vs. evil, male antagonists is pretty on-the-nose, dull and off-putting, which only manages to elicit an eye-roll. The heavy-handed virtue signalling yet again subverts any suspension of disbelief.

The story is a pretty run-of-the-mill “save the local savages” Avatar affair. A mediocre story can be saved by great characters… but I’ve seen toast with more personality than these supposed “characters”. To add insult to injury, much of the dialogue is slow beyond belief. For some arcane reason, much of the most pointless filler dialogues are stretched out to an absurd degree. And in many conversations, there’s an awkward silence where the camera lingers on certain shots for a few seconds too long, just enough to make you feel uncomfortable.

Especially after the first two games, and considering Lara has crawled through rivers of corpses, decapitated heads, limbs, rib cages, has murdered plenty of people and witnessed the supernatural, she really shouldn’t be as emotional as she is. So, the real question is: how can you merge the passionate yet naïve archaeologist/ explorer with the dispassionate executioner? You could explore the soft underbelly of Lara’s psyche: the regrets, doubts, apprehensions and fears she harbours after exposing herself to so much gruelling imagery. Give the whole thing a “Senua’s Sacrifice” spin. She’s stared death in the face innumerable times, and in turn exploring the heavy psychological toll it takes on her would be fascinating. Interestingly enough, this is exactly what the devs did in the “Nightmare” DLC, which was by far the most interesting content of the game story-wise. A real shame the DLC was so short and only scratched the surface of Lara’s mental state!

Despite all of the above, the saving grace of the game is the exploration: it’s wonderful. Every minute you’re discovering something new. The ancient Incan and Mayan aesthetics are fantastic and a real blast to explore. Puzzling together the various stories of what happened throughout the game universe via 400-year-old accounts and diaries left by pioneers of the old world is vastly more interesting than the main story and its cardboard characters. The majority of the tombs are a joy to explore, and each tomb has its own unique story to tell. Fantastic!

Despite all the criticisms, I consider SOTTR a great game worth your time.

I will say the the Lara Croft in 2013 is more mature then the one we got in shadow (which is honestly puzzling how a writer can go backwards). A prime example is when, in the reboot, two pilots bail out of a rescue plane after a failed rescue attempt. Just as Lara was about to go help the first pilot, Roth grabbed her and told her she shouldnt help the pilots as there was more at stake, than the pilots lives. He tried to lecture her that she only knows about loss, and doesnt know much about making hard choices. She replied with "Im not going to choose to let them die Roth".

(she acually gets annoyed at Jonah btw)

I could rant on and on but my biggest suggestion is, play tomb raider 2013, then play this. You will seriously laugh. Horrible writing but DECENT gameplay. Also the fact I had to look up what happened to Sam is really annoying. Rise should of covered this (same with the dual pistols), but they decided to put it into a novel. Good job.

summary: Its an OK game. Plenty to do (albeit alot of it being boring) but its semi enjoyable.

[h1] Review [/h1]

The Tomb Raider reboot trilogy is a perfect example of good games, full stop. To quote comrade Dyatlov: "not great, not terrible". This review will mainly be a take on the third installment but will cover the trilogy as a whole, as in my honest opinion there is not much reason to write separate reviews of them as you most likely will enjoy the whole trilogy if one is your fancy. This said, there are of course things that tell them apart. Shadow of the Tomb Raider is another respectable addition to the series which I can recommend if you are not discouraged by the inherent solidity, but more so staleness that the trilogy as a whole present.

Tomb Raider is at its core an action game, with formulaic shootouts and high-intensity chase sequences but has over the series evolved its open worlds and with it the adventurous tombs and puzzle solving. Stealth has always been prominent but mostly revolve around body stacking ("What was that sound?" "It came from over there" "Go look and I'll stay here" *stab* and repeat) or failed attempts at it which results in sloppy shootouts. Shadow of the Tomb Raider pride itself with an even greater focus on the badassery of the the Tomb Raider, thus implementing even more stealth sections, which comes down to smearing mud on yourself and hanging enemies from trees. Fine-tuning has been done throughout the series but the outcome has more or less been the same, resulting in gameplay that was fun on introduction, getting old as the first game came to a close and with the two followups a clear devotion to the beating of the dead horse that is Tomb Raider gameplay. Don't get me wrong, it is all very serviceable and mildly amusing. Furthermore it is good of the series to keep coherency between the titles, which is why I highlighted this review with the solidity of Tomb Raider.

Gunplay and crafting is adequate for the purpose. Progression is always the same, starting out with a bow and acquiring a handgun, assault rifle and shotgun as the game goes along. The puzzle tombs are easily the stars of the show, making use of gorgeous locations, satisfying progression and decent brain teasers but also suffers now and then from some inconsistencies in design, unoriginal pacing and tedious traversing. But this is something that follows the game throughout the linear story as well, with jaw-dropping set-pieces on one hand and dull enclosed battle arenas and slow climbing animations on the other. The more pressing conflict with the evolution of the franchise as a whole is the implementation of the RPG elements, something that can both be appreciated and criticized.

The first Tomb Raider was a very linear experience, with one crafting currency, some achievements, a few amount of tombs and little encouragement to revisit sites that had been passed. Rise of the Tomb Raider introduced a hub world of sort, a shop with in-game currency, hidden treasures, multiple crafting resources and an overabundance of loot and lore to rustle the jimmies of any completionist out there. Shadow expanded even further on these aspects. The question we have to ask ourselves is: what does this do with the game?

Well for one, there are more content to appreciate. More locations, lore and customization, which at first glance may seem as clear upgrades and an amplification of the experience. If there is more to enjoy there should be a greater effect. I don't have a distinct argument against open world gaming and quest inflation, but rather attribute my worries to a matter of taste. I do in fact encourage games that let you shape your own destiny and has a controlled amount of scope to both fill the void of RPG enthusiasts out there but also tell a concise story. The two Tomb Raider sequels instead tread into territory of campy quests of unimportance and an excess of fluff. Yes, you don't have to do these and the game can be played however you want, but the fact that they both distract from a smooth narrative and belittle the main story by making it less urgent is so very apparent. The story and its characters are not that well realized to begin with, but I would have condoned them if they had gone the whole way to depict a cheesy adventure flick instead of trying to enlarge something void of authenticity. It doesn't help the fact that dialogues with NPCs are so wooden with uncanny animations that the intrigued completionist that I am found myself skipping dialogues after I was halfway through the game. The same goes for relics, murals and records, that I sat down to hear the voice actor tell me about in the first game, but just skimmed through in the latter two.

This is the problem with the series, with solidity eventually transforming into staleness. This doesn't invalidate the quality of each game as they can all be appreciated in a vacuum, but as a coherent experience they do get gradually worse. On the other hand if we analyze respective setting, aesthetics and story some differences can be found. As a complete story with a set goal and strong characters I think Rise functions the best, while Shadow is obtuse and meandering and the first installment (although a strong starting point for the protagonist) fails to develop any other character or motive. Setting and aesthetics differ immensely obviously, with the Japanese influenced multi-faceted island of the first game, the snowy Byzantine second and the South American jungles of the third. Rise has gorgeous snow and ice effects and some incredible set-pieces, but when doing inquires about what people found visually great about Rise I found out (as I already knew myself) that the only truly memorable locations were the Syria mission and the shipwreck in the ice (which are very early on in the game). This is my biggest problem with Rise, as many of the locations do feel rather drab and barren because of being set in Siberia. The fact is the game only became more and more dull the longer it went, with a very unsatisfying conclusion to boot. Shadow instead practically reeks of adventure feel à la Indiana Jones, revolving around Central and South American traditions with lush jungles and very exquisite and original tombs. With this I do not mean that every Tomb Raider is better set in exotic jungles, but I think Rise serves its purpose as a palette cleanser and means of variation. Nevertheless, the vibrant environment of Shadow is a much more immersive experience and believable depiction of tomb raiding and would have been my go-to of the series if not for the fact that the 2013 reboot excels in pretty much every aspect.

The first game has already become quite dated in terms of graphics and some stylistic choices do jump out as odd compared to the sequels, but as a gaming experience, abundance of memorable locations, aesthetics and conclusive dramaturgy, Tomb Raider (2013) stands supreme. But that shouldn't stop you from playing the sequels. My take on it is, if you like a linear story with great aesthetic choices play Tomb Raider. If you want RPG elements, great villains and snow, play Rise of the Tomb Raider. If you want the best graphics, tombs and biggest bang for the buck, play Shadow of the Tomb Raider.

Although initially groundbreaking and thrilling, the Tomb Raider reboot trilogy can in the end be summarized as nothing more than a blockbuster d1ck flick. Not bad, but won't stay very long in your mind.

[h1]Thoughts on Game Play[/h1]
Shadow of the Tomb Raider (SotTR) has the signature rock climbing and parkour elements from the previous games, but keeps it fresh. The rappelling mechanic that allows Lara to drop down from high places makes the level design feel different from previous games, not only can you go up, but also down.

Weapons are not too different from previous games, but I like the different types of arrows that Lara can learn to craft. For example a hallucinogenic arrow (learned later in the story) that causes enemies to become paranoid and randomly shoot, causing friendly fire casualties.

Once again the stealth mechanics are great, from being able to kill from tree branches, hide in foliage, now Lara can cover herself in mud to hide in nature. Ledge takedowns and stealth from under water are also super fun. The extensive ways for stealth makes me try to complete the fight levels with stealth. I even restarted checkpoints multiple times just to fully stealth kill, as if I were playing Dishonoured.

[h1]Thoughts on Story / Lara[/h1]
SotTR explores Lara's backstory more. Combined with the "Blood Ties" DLC in Rise of the Tomb Raider, I feel we get to see more of Lara's anguish over the death of her family from such a young age. I don't feel there's a lot of resolution - even as an adult we see that the trauma affects her a lot. And sometimes that's just how it is. She tries to live as well as she can, but there is no "magic solution". She's still figuring things out in this game, which I find brings her down to a relatable, human level.

Even though she kills a lot, gets angry when her allies are hurt or killed, and then takes it out on enemies, she gets called out on it. Jonah calls her out for thinking she's the hero, and her enemies call her out for being hypocritical when Lara condemns them for killing. They point out Lara has killed so many as well.

I like that SotTR's environments are more lively - the three main towns are full of people. Even if I didn't find the side characters' backstories very engaging, the fact that there are so many more people to interact with made me more invested in the story, compared to Rise of the Tomb Raider, which was very bleak. Maybe the snow in RotTR reminds me too much of Canadian winters...

I wouldn't say the main story is very good - it's average and often has story conveniences (relic gets stolen, clue leads to dead end, then find another clue, which leads to another dead end, rinse and repeat). But it works to tie the game together and I actually remember SotTR's story more than RotTR's.

[h1]Exploration[/h1]
I am a big fan of SotTR because of the varied and unique tombs. There's so much to do - from challenge tombs Lara gets skills that can't be earned elsewhere, and crypts where you can find legendary outfits from ancient warriors in the lore.

The tombs themselves feel very different from each other, with very detailed environments and architecture. I think compared to RotTR the devs really have outdone themselves in this regard. And I'm only talking about the challenge tombs in the main game, not including the new ones coming as DLC. Overall I'm very impressed with the tomb and crypt exploration in SotTR and it's a big part of my playtime in this game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
I found it worth it to purchase day one, but of course if you're not playing it immediately just wait and get on sale. The unique and detailed tombs already gave me my money's worth. The environments are lovely and I sometimes just walk slow in the towns to take it all in.

If you liked the previous games for the exploration, tombs and puzzles, I think SotTR is the best one. If you just want more of the same, this game will scratch that itch as well. If you were kind of indifferent towards the previous reboot games, then this one probably won't change your mind. Overall, this is the first time I've paid $80 Canadian dollars (curse inflation!!!) for a game and immediately found it worth it!

This game isn't bad, it just isn't nearly as good as Rise of the Tomb Raider. And since the Steam rating scale is Yes or No on a recommendation, I can't recommend this when a better game already exists. From the transition of the first Tomb Raider to Rise of the Tomb Raider they added so many things that improved the overall quality of the game and built upon survival and the combat. With Shadow, it seems like they just subtracted everything that was good about the previous two games and left us with a subpar, poorly designed experience.

To give you an idea of how poorly this game was designed compared to the previous two, there's a skill tree that's split into 3 eqaul parts. How about Lara, a woman who is known for reading and deciphering numerous languages, learns how to speak the native language and interact with the people?

I still got a decent amount of fun out of this game, but my mind keeps wandering back to Rise of the Tomb Raider. I 100% completed that game, but I feel like putting down Shadow of the Tomb Raider so I can go finish the achievements I never got in the superior game.

[h1][b]Overview[/b][/h1]
Shadow of the Tomb Raider (SoTTR) is the latest entry in the Tomb Raider franchise. This game aims to conclude Lara Croft's adventure that started with the original 2013 Tomb Raider. The game is a story-driven singleplayer game with interesting combat mechanics, however, does this game stand out from the last two entries? And how good is this game compared to the previous ones?

[h1][b]Graphics and Audio[/b][/h1]
Shadow of the Tomb Raider is one of the best looking games I've played in a while, it has breathtaking visuals and I don't think I've been this immersed in a game since Kingdom Come: Deliverance. The game has a near-photorealistic rendering of foliage, skin, and lighting. There were points where I thought I was watching a live-action cutscene due to the way the character models were rendered. The audio is another aspect SoTTR gets right, the sounds when you're deep in the jungles of Peru are so immersive and on point that it adds a whole layer of realism. The music is fantastic and really adds to the mood of the situation, the soundtrack when you're deep underwater changes to a more frantic beat when you're running out of oxygen and this adds so much tension it's fantastic. Both the visuals and the sounds work together to make a very immersive and believable experience that is simply incredible
[b]10/10[/b]

[h1][b]Gameplay[/b][/h1]
Shadow tried something very interesting for this entry and that was reducing the number of combat encounters and increasing the number of things to explore. While this might not be for everyone I absolutely think this is a fantastic choice as we get to raid more tombs and explore the masterfully crafted world. This change in focus really adds a lot of replayability due to the all the things that there are to explore. I am currently on my second playthrough and I'm still discovering new skills and abilities. The combat is more refined than ever with a large emphasis on stealth, now Lara can cover her self in mud to hide from thermal cameras, hide in wall vines, and be a lot more brutal than she was in the previous games, however, this game does have annoying bosses that require too many shots to kill and have a lot of enemies that rush you at once. 
[b]9/10[/b]

[h1][b]Story[/b][/h1]
The story in this game provides closure to the overall story arc but it could've gone so much further than it actually went. This entry to the series solidifies the idea that there are consequences for the careless raiding Lara has gone through in the last two games. She is faced with the consequences of her actions throughout the entire game and this really pushes Lara to evolve and become a stronger hero in the story. The story was enjoyable but I think they could've made it longer or maybe added another explorable area or expanding the starting area. 
[b]8/10[/b]

[h1][b]Performance, Bugs, and Glitches[/b][/h1]
SoTTR is not a flawless game, it has a handful of bugs which I noticed during my playtime. There was a noticeable stutter during parts of the game where no matter how high my frame rate was. I have a GTX 1070 Ti, I7 8700, and 16 GBs of RAM and I still had these stutters sometimes. I did maintain above 60 FPS at all times which is an improvement over the last game. This game is very optimized and I had no problem maxing it out. Another bug that was very annoying was that sometimes Lara would fall through the floor when having to swing and it would lead to my death. One thing that annoyed me was how many outfits the game has to offer but you're restricted to this ugly Incan robe for a majority of the game. I think the game should not restrict which outfit I use especially if I have a good combo going that has a lot of benefits towards my gameplay experience. 
[b]7/10[/b]

[h1][b]Conclusion[/b][/h1]
Shadow of the Tomb Raider is a fantastic final entry to the trilogy of Tomb Raider games. The game looks and sounds amazing and easily immersed me in the game world. The gameplay is fantastic and has decent replayability but it would be nice to have a little bit more action sequences to allow players to use their abilities they have spent leveling up. The story works well but I think there was a lot of wasted potential to make the game longer and more enjoyable but I think it served its purpose in concluding the game. The game had some bugs here and there but it did not distract from the overall experience of the game. So should you get this game? I think if you've played the other two you should definitely get this game as it is a fantastic entry to the saga, however, if you haven't played the other two games you should try those out to get a better understanding of the story and of the story of the rebooted Lara Croft.
[b]8.5/10[/b]

After going through this trilogy reboot in a week and beating all the main story content, I truly have to say that this series of the reboot tomb raider games have to truly be the best 3 games I have played back to back in a very long time, I wish I got to it alot sooner than waiting years to play them. All 3 of these games were not missing at all the story, combat everything about a game just gets better and better each game you play, they are all bangers and filled with amazing thriller moments.

Shadow of the tomb raider isn't the best game to end a trilogy on, it has some of the best aspects but ultimately is the weakest of the survivor trilogy. I still enjoy playing it but it is my least replayed due to some pacing issues, a genuinely terrible story with wooden chracters and some annoying design decisions. 

The good is that this game tries to go for a more isolated tomb raider experience, whilst it's still nowhere near the originals in terms of atmosphere it's at least nice to feel more tomb raider and less uncharted. 

Combat feels quite a bit more fleshed out, stealth is massively improved and lara goes full rambo in this game, it's really quite nice stealth killing an enemy from a grassy wall and then quickly jumping out to headshot everyone.

Her annoying sidekick also starts getting sick of her shit and I feel Jonas is a window for the players to express how dumb lara is being. If it was only lara's questionable actions that was the issue then this would be more forgivable but this story is just so bland and forgettable that it borders on offensive, look at rise of the tomb raider, that games story sucked but at least it was interesting with the Russian Jesus plot, this game is just bad man wants thing for reasons and lara will go to extreme lengths to stop bad man.

If you've enjoyed previous versions of Tomb Raider then you are bound to enjoy this one, and to some extent, that's the problem with this game.  But first, the pros:
Graphics - excellent, but not 'next gen'.  There's a lack of detail in Lara's interactions with her surroundings that detracts from being immersed in the game. 8/10
Sound - excellent.  No issues for me. 10/10
Controls - very good.  There's the odd annoyance with an unavailable camera angle that makes finding the next hand-hold awkward, and has lead to a death while trying something that was wrong, but it's been a small issue twice. 9/10
In fact, purely as a game (in the retro sense), I can't really fault this title, with the exception that I have to agree with another reviewer that mentioned a lack of need to increase Lara's skills.  Perhaps, if you need to shave a few minutes of your speed run, then being able to take less damage in hand-to-hand combat will be necessary, but playing the title as an 'experience' (that is, a one-off play through with a desire to be immersed in story), then I'd have to say that so far I'm not feeling the need.
As far as the puzzles go they're standard Tomb Raider fare.  That's not a bad thing,  Yes, it would have been nice to have just a little more diversity in the way that Lara can solve puzzles, or indeed, how the puzzles are solved.  Pull this, push that, jump over the other, it's difficult to criticise this stuff, after all, it's a Tomb Raider title, what did I expect?
So, as far as the playability side of this title goes I'd give it 9/10.

It's when it comes to modern-day immersion that  I find 'Shadow' to be sadly lacking anything really new, so far at least(I've only played it for 30 hours, and I'm at best half way through).

As far as immersion and story go I'm finding it difficult to care about Lara herself. She seems to be quite a whinny, spoilt brat, who seems to care little for indigenous culture as long as her quest can be advanced.  This might be ok, if it's used as a deliberate part of showing how Lara grows as she makes her way through her adventure, but I'm not seeing that so far, and there are a lot of cliches in both her character and events that befall her.  Good storytelling doesn't need to force the action, it happens as a natural consequence of events.  

In the original 2013 Tomb Raider, I found myself connecting well with Lara's character, and caring about what happened to her.  In 'Shadow', I find myself thinking of her like any other murderous, first-person shooter character, which means I don't think of her much at all.  I only use the avatar as a means to carry out the necessary killing required to complete any particular quest.

Opportunities for really good story telling have been missed here, unfortunately.

This title needs to go some to achieve a 10 out of 10 rating in today's gaming world, where I'm judging games pretty much in the same way I judge movies.  All the SFX in the world can't make a bad movie good, it still needs a good story, and characters, and although games still have more leeway than movies, a AAA title needs to view itself in the same way if it's to get the plaudits, and Shadow of the Tomb Raider does not.
I bought this title on sale at half-price, and I'm quite happy with that.  I'd be less happy had I paid full price.

[b]Final mark out of 10, 7.[/b]

I have played the Tomb Raider games since the original in 1996 (bought the pyramid shaped box at Sams Club). I think I have played every major PC game, but not all of the spin-offs (e.g. I seem to recall a Diablo-like version that I never tried). Every one of them involved at least one frustrating aspect, such as jumping in an unexpected direction, irritating timed sequences that had to be done perfectly, interactive movies that had to be done perfectly, etc. This one has some aspects of those, but not nearly as bad and not enough to detract from the overall stunning graphics, good story, music, etc. This is one of the best, which makes sense, as it is the most recent and seems to have taken all of the past frustrations and lessons learned into account. To be clear, I do not expect perfection. This is an extremely complex game that I can not even begin to imagine how much coding effort went into getting everything right. I have been a computational science/physics programmer for my ~25 year career and still cannot wrap my mind around the coding that must be involved in a complex game like this.

Best part of the trilogy and big step in the right direction!
Bigger and alive world with more tombs, puzzles are challenging (at least on "One with the jungle" difficulty) and exploration feels more organic, new crafting materials and skill system, also massively improved stealth mechanics from previus games  with beautiful graphics and fun story.
Some things could be better (combat, animations, side missions), but the overall experience is excellent.

As much as I hate to say it, for me this is the most disappointing game in the Tomb Raider reboot trilogy. There are many problems with this game, but the two most important are its story and its stale mechanics. 

Lara being completely unlikable is perhaps the biggest reason why Shadow's story failed. Lara is no longer the desperate young woman stranded after a shipwreck who was so easy to empathize with in the original reboot. She is now a bloodthirsty killer with an unhealthy obsession towards destroying a generic evil organization. But I don't dislike Lara because she is now a killing machine, I dislike her because a killing machine is all she is. In order for a player to be invested in a story, they must be invested in its characters. The original Tomb Raider reboot made players feel sympathetic to Lara by making her a victim of violence and hardship. But as she grew in strength in each game, she has found nothing else to hook players with. In Shadow of the Tomb Raider, she is not a victim anymore, instead, she is nothing. She has no character: she never cracks jokes, she talks in a monotonous voice, and her decisions are generic... She is a shadow (heh) of the older Lara that a generation of gamers fell in love with. As a result, every scene containing Lara in this game (a.k.a every scene in the game) feels dry. Combined with forgettable allies and villains, an insistence on unneccessarily dark themes, and a complete lack of levity, Shadow of the Tomb Raider's story could not engage or let alone interest me in any way. 

Gameplay wise, the game is almost identical to 2015's Rise and 2013's original. Tomb Raider (2013)'s mechanics were fun and exciting when the game released, though it's combat system was relatively weak. Rise of the Tomb Raider lifted it's gameplay almost 1:1 from Tomb Raider (2013), but it's massively improved graphics helped add some novelty. Shadow of the Tomb Raider adds almost nothing to the table gameplay wise, but more importantly does nothing to fix the glaring problems with its existing mechanics. Combat is immensly frustrating: enemies are far too tanky and don't even flinch when shot, close quarters encounters (almost all combat scenarios) do not suit most of Lara's arsenal, the cover system is unreliable etc. Even the traversal mechanics are showing it's age: Lara's movements feel floaty and sometimes imprecise, difficult jumps are made even harder by bad geometry that stop Lara in midair... All of these are problems that were also present in the previous game, but I expected them to be fixed 3 years later considering there are no massive graphical leaps this time around.

By the end of this game, Lara's origin story is over and she is ready to embark on a fresh new journey with the skills of the true Tomb Raider. Hopefully by the next time we see her, she will also have the charm and character of the true Tomb Raider, and the gameplay behind her will be as excellent as a Tomb Raider game deserves to be.

First, I really like the previous two other Tomb Raider games but this one was meh. I have been on a Lara Croft binge for over a month now and Shadow of the Tomb Raider is my favorite. In a word, this game is magnificent. On occasion, I stand in awe of the creativity and programming that is required to build a game and this is one of those times.

The story takes place in Peru and focuses on the indigenous culture (past and present). You have the jungle, spectacular ruins, ancient technology, primitive villages, and political intrigue. And, as usual, Lara is on a heroic quest with Jonah to take down Trinity.

SoTR introduces climbing on overhangs that is fun and dizzying. I played the game on the easiest level (for combat, puzzles, and exploration) and this was about perfect for me. I still fell to my death on countless occasions but I am certainly  more coordinated now than I was before.  I played with a controller until combat. Then, switched to a keyboard/mouse for better aim.  I do not believe I could have navigated the complexities of this environment with only a keyboard/mouse. 

There is a plethora of resources to collect for crafting potions, ammunition, and repairing vestige garments. Using the potions to strengthen Lara's focus and endurance was a big help. Additional resources such as gold and jade can be traded with local merchants for gear and anything else you might be missing. The game includes countless collectibles (relics and documents) that create a library of story lore and cultural history.

Puzzles focus on working through diverse environments using complicated ancient machinery (levers, towers, gas jets, water wheels, to name a few). While paths are usually clearly marked (in easy mode), the complexities of the challenge tombs were amazing. On more than one occasion, I used Stella's Tomb Raider web site to figure out my starting point.

Although there are long periods where you can explore at your leisure, there are quite a few enemies to defeat and wild beasts to hunt. Much of this can be handled with a stealthy approach and there is something quite satisfying about hiding high on a tree branch and taking out unaware enemies with a bow and poison-tipped arrows! In one section, you lose your weapons and must defeat a series of hostiles with only a knife and your ability to blend into the environment.

As with the first two Tomb Raider games, my problem came at the end with the need to defeat an almost impossibly difficult boss.  I did complete the main story but still have open side missions related to 5 DLC challenge tombs. So, my journey with Lara is far from over. 

I highly recommend SoTR to adventurers. If you are hard-core, the difficulty of the game can be increased. If not, there is no shame in taking the easier route. Like its predecessor (Rise of the Tomb Raider), SoTR is so big that it can't be fully absorbed in a single play through.  The 'New Game+' feature allows you to restart with some of your earned gear and skills and is a nice way to jump back in to experience more.

Shadow of the Tomb Raider is the third and weakest entry in the rebooted Tomb Raider trilogy. The first game excelled at telling a tight, well-paced origin story, while the second expanded on the gameplay and world. If you are new to the series, I highly recommend you go with either of those games, they are both excellent experiences. 

That being said, if you have played both the previous games and loved them like I did, you’ll probably like this one as well, just not as much. Here are a few points to consider if you're having trouble deciding whether to pick this up,  

[*] My biggest gripe with the game is the writing. The story on offer is abysmal, pretty much all the characters except for Lara are flat and boring. The side quests are a bit more varied and interesting than Rise, but overall nothing special
[*] The combat is mostly identical to Rise (and far less frequent) 
[*] Traversal and exploration has been expanded upon with the addition of the grapple hook but its nothing ground breaking. The jungle setting might be my favourite in the series, however the environments are far less diverse than Rise and they can get a bit samey the more you play. Exploration overall is quite fun  
[*] The tombs here are the best in the series; the puzzles are challenging, the atmosphere and visual design is excellent and some of them are really large 
[*] The outfit selection is quite poor; a majority of them are tribal outfits that aren’t really that interesting. You are also forced to wear these for a significant portion of the game
[*] It has a photo mode, honestly might be the best new feature they introduced 

Overall, as a fan of the reboot trilogy, Shadow is a bit of a disappointment. However, if you are a big fan of the series, I’d still recommend this, probably pick it up on sale.

First off let me say that while this is a negative review, SotTR is not a terrible game. It's a well polished AAA that just happens to have enough issues to make it a disappointing end to the reboot trilogy. Steam does not let me rate a game out of 10 and I'm unwilling to give it a thumbs up, so here we are.

Let's start with what the game does well. The environmental design in this game is superb. The variation isn't huge because there's no globe hopping in this game (you'll be seeing a lot of jungle,) but the attention to detail and art direction meant I never cared. This is a beautiful game to look at.

Moving onto gameplay, this is where things become a bit more mixed. On the good side of things the platforming is as fluid as the previous two games, but more importantly, Eidos have finally managed to get the 'right' amount of actual tomb raiding into the game. Tomb Raider 2013 really suffered for having really poor tombs that felt like little more than small caves with basic physics puzzles. Crystal Dynamics improved this a fair bit in Rise of the Tomb Raider with longer tombs and more complex puzzles (even if the theming of the tombs wasn't always very tomb-like). With Shadow of the Tomb Raider we're finally back to something fans of the pre-reboot games might recognize. Really lengthy tombs with complex multi-stage puzzles. I really can't understate how much better this aspect of the game is compared to the previous two.

The problems with the gameplay start to become apparent a few hours in when you realise that you're almost getting too much of a good thing. Whereas the previous reboot games would intersperse sections of tomb raiding and exploration with gun fights, the combat in SotTR has been seriously reduced. And when I say reduced I mean that other than a couple of dudes near the start, you won't be shooting anything other than guinea pigs and parrots for the first two thirds of the game. I can see why this has happened; the previous two reboot games got flak from some quarters for having too much gun-play. Personally I enjoyed those sections in TR2013 and RotTR and don't think they had too much shooting, they just had too little tomb raiding. This lack of combat becomes a real problem because it means that the tomb raiding and exploration sections of SotTR are just too long. What is actually really good gameplay when looked at by itself becomes tedious and repetitive. Something I really should have been enjoying was starting to make me feel bored.

Worse than the lack of combat is the fact that what little combat does exist is just not very good. Eidos have introduced some new stealth mechanics and seem hell bent on forcing you to use them. You can now hide in bushes growing up walls which isn't really any different from hiding in bushes on the ground, it's just a new animation. You can also cover yourself in mud to hide from night vision goggles. There are three (I think,) instances in the game where you can use the mud mechanic. The mud patches are placed right at the entrance to a zone, to the point where you can't really progress to the combat without covering yourself in mud. You're given so little agency over this mechanic and it seems to make so little difference to the gameplay that I can't really figure out why they bothered to include it. My only guess is that they had something similar in the advertising cinematic so felt they needed to include it in the game.

The enemy AI is clearly tuned towards the player using stealth. If you break cover they have pinpoint accuracy. Not that you will anyway because there are sections of the game where despite actually still having all your weapons (you haven't had them stripped or lost them down a waterfall or anything,) the game will only let you stealth kill with your knife. Unfortunately killing in stealth isn't particularly fun either since the AI is as dumb as a bag of rocks. If you've ever maxed out stealth in Skyrim and had an enemy NPC not see you as you crouch right next to them and the corpse of their buddy, you'll know what I'm talking about. It might seem like I'm talking about the combat in this game a lot but it really is just such a massive step backwards compared to the previous two games.

Combat is not the only problem with the gameplay though some of the others are directly related to it. The talent tree for example is lifted almost wholesale from Rise. Ninety percent of those talents are combat related and are therefore useless for most of the game. This really hinders any feeling of character progression. The crafting system likewise suffers since it's focused on upgrading weapons and armour which will rarely be used. The armour sets in the game do at least have some non-combat bonuses which improve yields on foraging and the like. However the main hub of the game will force you to use a disguise costume which has no bonuses at all. Yes, you read that right. You will spend the game earning armour sets which you then can't use for large sections of it.

Lastly, lets talk about the story. I'll be brief to avoid spoilers. It's not very good.

To be fair, the reboot games have never had the strongest writing but it has always been 'good enough'. TR2013 had the most cohesive narrative since it was almost entirely self contained. Rise expanded on the role of Trinity and offered quite a lot of backstory if you read all the collectable documents. SotTR has very little set up. You get a McGuffin waved in your face at the start of the game by Trinity and then you won't see it or them again until the final third. The time in between is filled with Lara's introspection on her life and journey so far. It has the potential to really build her character but really just comes across as a bit whiny and self centred. By far the most relatable character is her friend Jonah, almost to the point where I was wishing he was the protagonist.

The 'big bad' in SotTR is the biggest let down. We've had two games building up Trinity as some world spanning illuminati type organisation and yet the 'big bad' feels so loosely connected to them. I think you could probably remove all references to Trinity from the game and it would make no difference to the character of 'big bad'. Considering this is the final instalment in the trilogy it feels like it offers zero closure when it come to the main antagonists of the series.

[h1][b]Shadow of the Tomb Raider[/b][/h1]
[i]Shadow of the Tomb Raider[/i] is an action-adventure game in which Lara Croft tries to save the world from a Maya apocalypse. 

[b]Story[/b]

The story begins very Tomb Raider like, Lara Croft tries to stop Trinity once more but ultimately fails and a chain of apocalypse like events start to happen. It’s time for the player to stop Trinity once and for all, while discovering new places and trying to stop a Maya disaster from happening. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2488787538
[b]Personal Note[/b]

I picked this game up on a sale and I’m honestly not disappointed. Gameplay wise nothing much really changed – which is a bit unfortunate, that being said, it’s very easy to pick up especially if you played the other two Tomb Raider games in this reboot installment. 

I found myself completing all the side quests and there are quite a handful of those – I would say that most of them seem to be optional, to some extend at least, but at the same time they unlock certain areas that you wouldn’t be able to access otherwise. If you don’t care about collectibles or side quests you can easily ignore them without that much of a punishment. 

Although there is more positive than negative to this game, I want to mention that this game unfortunately suffers from some weird decisions like the outfit system and how the game forces you to move slower when talking with someone on the move or while walking through random areas.
 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2790580288
The photo mode is pretty decent and for sure one of the better ones out there – so if you like to  take screenshots you are good to go. You can use the photo mode in cut scenes as well. 

[b]Rating[/b]
[list][b]Pros[/b]
[*] Beautiful graphics
[*] Great sound design 
[*] Good main story
[*] Interesting side stories
[*] Good voice acting from the main characters
[*] A lot of stuff to do if you’re interested in 100%
[*] DLC Tombs are pretty decent
[*] Great photo mode
[/list]
[list][b]Cons[/b]
[*] Puzzles are too easy
[*] Controls are not perfect for keyboard & mouse
[*] Just a few new mechanics
[*] Voice acting of side characters seem a bit off
[*] Forced walking at times
[*] Game breaking bug if you shoot a laptop
[*] Optimization isn’t too great in the bigger areas
[*] The outfit system is pretty weird & annoying
[/list]
[b]Conclusion[/b]
 
Well, the question is: Is [i]Shadow of the Tomb Raider[/i] worth getting? If you like action-adventures or if you’re a big Tomb Raider fan you can’t do anything wrong with buying the game. I’d recommend waiting for a sale in which the whole bundle is a bit cheaper – mostly because the story itself isn’t too long if you don’t do any of the side quests or optional tombs or DLC tombs. 

All in all, I think it’s a good game and I hope that the possible 4th game in this new Tomb Raider franchise comes with more new mechanics and gameplay elements and more challenges that are a bit harder to complete.
