Ten years ago, we got a brand new, youthful Lara. This fragile girl, then still unsullied by the dangerous adventure, did not go far for the pained cries. But she toughens up fairly quickly, and we watch her transform into the fearless killing machine we knew before over the course of three new episodes. In Shadow of the Tomb Raider, there is no doubt that we are dealing with a mature Miss Croft.
Those who are looking forward to revolutionary changes should lower their expectations. Shadow of the Tomb Raider is not supposed to push the boundaries. His goal is to complete the story of the birth of the most famous tomb robber in the most entertaining way possible. And if it worked so great last time, why change it anyway, right? So, the new Lara goes more or less over the copier at important points, but that doesn't mean she's completely scared of the news. You don't have a flood of surprises waiting for you, just a slightly more refined experience in several directions.
Just looking at the new Lara and her surroundings is breathtaking. The dense jungle creates a natural impression of impenetrability, while the screeching monkeys, singing birds and insect-filled undergrowth will leave you in no doubt: you are in an absolute wilderness where no human foot has set foot for a good 300 years.

But this beautiful jungle will soon be tainted by the blood of self-sacrificing soldiers of the fanatical Trinity group, with which our heroine has been struggling for some time. As is often the case with villains, their sense of preservation of monuments is somehow lacking. Where Lara uses logic to open a hundred-ton door, the villainous organizations reach for dynamite. And yet they never find what they seek.
It is Lara who, after solving several puzzles, gets to the key in the shape of a dagger, which Trinity craves like a chicken for flux. Although she gets to him first, she forgot to do her homework this time. Dr. Dominguez himself, the arch-enemy, must initiate her into the new events.
By picking up the dagger, Lara set in motion a real apocalypse predicting devastating floods, strong storms and earthquakes. You can be very hardened, but this kind of news just blows you away. So shadows begin to fall on Lara's reputation, while you breathlessly watch a disaster of enormous proportions, which you yourself unknowingly unleashed.
This essentially makes Lara the villain, and I won't lie to you when I say that Pedro Dominguez is a badass. After a long time, we have an antagonist who has all five together. His intentions are pure, only good. And not just for him. Exactly opposite. You don't have a choice in the game, but you are fighting an internal battle. Both the protagonist and the villain both want to do the greatest good, but each on a completely different front, although neither necessarily on the wrong front.

The classic treasure hunt was a great ride that I will remember fondly. Especially the scene when Lara finally runs out of patience. [b] 75% [/b]

Most of us long time and old time fans of the Tomb Raider series will feel quite moved at times while playing Shadow of the Tomb Raider. Lara meets lethal piranhas, annoying bats, friendly monkeys, deadly eels - all that kind of fauna that we were so used to seeing in Lara's classic adventures. There is also a vast jungle, hugely improved over the unforgettable Tomb Raider 3 one, and of course there is Peru and its folklore, which brings vivid memories of the first Tomb Raider ever to mind. The nostalgia factor is rather strong in the latest installment of the series, which, although it reaches certain heights of perfection in some fields, somehow slightly fails to deliver its full raiding power.

The story is interesting but unfortunately unfolds too quickly and somewhat superficially. Although the Latin American & Mayan themes are showcased extremely well, the plot itself is too weak to support a whole game. The idea of a lost tribe that is living in its own isolated corner, away from the so-called civilized world, is very intricate, but one would expect a lot more elaboration under the surface - because visually, the presentation is close to perfection. Lara arrives at the hidden city of Paititi and discovers a paradise on earth, but soon finds out that even paradises have their troubles. There is a dethroned queen, a power-hungry antagonist, usurpers, rebels; gruesome sacrifices take place, people are held and tortured in prison cells. All this sounds extremely interesting, the characters involved however are largely one-dimensional, and you do not have the chance to get to know them well enough so as to feel for them (with the exception of Lara and her old buddy Jonah). Which is a pity, as there are certain things that could have been elaborated a lot more. For example, I got very strong "Heart of Darkness" vibes (I refer to the classic novella by Joseph Conrad) when I saw Dr Dominguez in his impressive tribal outfit the moment that Lara realized that her number one enemy was actually a royal Maya descendant - a theme that should have been given more time and depth.

That said, the story somehow manages to surprisingly build up as soon as the last section starts, and the finale is quite epic on its own, although I still think that Lara's arch enemy should have been present a lot more throughout the story up to that point. Just remember Constantin from Rise of the Tomb Raider - he was an ever powerful villain whose ominous presence was always threatening everyone and everything even when he was not around. Dr Dominguez comes off as a confused, marginally deranged idiot with no convincing motivation for his actions. Similarly, Queen Unuratu leaves the game as discreetly as she joins it and as soon as she is out, you almost forget about her. Crimson Fire, however, is an unforgettable figure, in spite of her brief role.

Nonetheless, if you are a fan of exploring, you are going to have the time of your life with Shadow of the Tomb Raider. The sceneries are massive, and there is something to look for in almost every impossible corner. I was very close to reaching the game's final mission when I thought I'd fast travel a bit to check a couple of things. The couple of things became a dozen and soon I realized that I couldn't care less (so to speak) about the story, getting more and more fascinated with the lushly designed and tantalizing settings that were constantly inviting me to explore them in every detail.

Tomb Raider has always been primarily about exploration and discovery, and Shadow of the Tomb Raider is impeccable from this aspect. The gameplay is perfectly set up, so that you can reach the point-of-no-return campsite and go back to explore every nook and cranny before you proceed, thanks to the Fast Travel system. Of course there are tombs. And not simply that. The tombs of Shadow of the Tomb Raider are majestic, they are nearly mini-games themselves, they are something incredible. Same goes for a main key mission, that of San Juan. Everything concerning that mission is magnificently done - from the sceneries to the puzzles, from the music to the overall atmosphere. There are also lots of challenges, some of which are fun to do (like the one which involves rope-pulling pink frog totems) and some of which will have you looking around for stuff to do and items to find. Lara also has the option to help out people in assigned missions. These are optional, but if she does carry them out, she will be rewarded with gifts and XP.

Shadow of the Tomb Raider is an awesome game in some ways but unfortunately not in others. The developers really tried to create a cool final game in this trilogy. In many ways it is the definitive Tomb Raider game as they took most of the things that make the series good and turned them up to eleven. They have designed things in ways that make it easy to get immersed and explore more below the surface if you want too (quite literally sometimes). There are a lot of underwater areas in this game which are excellent and maybe the best parts of the game. There’s also a huge hub area called Paititi which looks fantastic and is loaded with things to find and do.

This game is really beautiful, they even managed to make Lara look good again compared to the last game in the trilogy at least. She still doesn’t look all that great though but at least her player model is well rendered. Seriously this game looks amazing, the graphics alone make it worth playing. Some of the sequences in the tombs are also very intense and the climbing sequences are a lot of fun. The gameplay and the level design are very well designed and in this respect Shadow of the Tomb Raider is as good as any other modern AAA game. 

However it’s with the characters and the story that this game is actually pretty awful. The story and cutscenes are more boring than ever for this series and I actually just started skipping them completely about half way through the campaign. The most interesting thing about the story is just the environment and how deep into the jungle you end up going. Other than this it is a slow, boring slog through the main story. This is made even worse by the fact that Lara is an annoying and boring character in this game. 

It’s cool how in the previous game, Rise of the Tomb Raider, they included some missions in Croft Manor. In those missions the developers gave some back story about Lara as a child and in this game they expand on that a little bit. Even though the story and cutscenes really suck in these sequels at least the developers were trying to create some immersion here. 

Unfortunately though the vast majority of the story is terrible all over again just like the previous game, it’s very boring and even depressing at times. In fact I find it hard to understand how they couldn't have hired some good writers or something to improve this aspect of the game. I do recommend this game because of the level design and the gameplay but it is a shame (just like the previous game in the series) that the story really sucks.

This is the most mature of the three. Fitting because its the last in the trilogy. By mature I mean the themes and world this game takes you. It's not meant to appeal to kids who just want non-stop action. It's meant for someone with a curiosity in different cultures. There is also a higher difficulty, I feel, with the tombs. Shadow feels matured because it feels complete.

While I do think Rise is an overall better game for the masses, objectively the presentation of Shadow tops it. There is so much cultural background there is a noticeable slow-down to the pacing because you end up doing other things. But that's not to say that there isn't action either. Rest assured there is a good balance of action.

The team did an incredible job doing research related to Mesoamerican mythology. It's spectacular how much detail they put into the game, down to the dialects, the spanish (accurate sounding speakers), the costumes, architecture, village areas, creative tombs... it goes on.

Also I'd like to give extra honors to the sound design using native instruments to convey the culture while still doing modern cinematics. The ambient sounds and tense music is amazing.

I just finished the game and I thoroughly enjoyed it. I'm surprised I haven't played this sooner.
Not a bad game, but it doesn’t generate the same excitement and feels more boring to play than the previous 2 games in the series. it’s still okay for a couple of evenings.

in this game the focus was clearly put on cinematics and direction. the characters feel more believable, more realistic, and it’s much easier to emotionally trust them.

but in exchange for all of that, the game completely lost its original charm. there’s no longer that amazing level design, interesting tombs or excitement from exploring the world. the game basically turned into a regular story-driven experience.

weapon and skill progression - meh. i never actually felt the need to upgrade much even on hard mode. there was this constant feeling that the game got heavily casualized to attract a bigger audience.

yeah, the game looks beautiful and the cinematography is great. the story is dynamic, compact and the characters are well developed. but for every thing that got better, something else got worse.

i love this series too much to leave a negative review, but i really hope the developers will understand their strengths and weaknesses better when making Legacy of Atlantis.

This game feels like the developers took all the mechanics from the previous games in this series and reimplemented them without understanding them at all. So you're left with a mishmash of worthless game design elements that don't work more than half of the time.

The item system feels worthless. For the most part the initial guns in the game are more than adequate and upgrading the others to see their final specs ends up being a major waste of time. I really wish I hadn't spent so much time in the game playing the gathering-everything-on-the-screen-and-sell-it-game. The game probably would have been much more fun without using the Lara sense all the time to make sure I didn't miss anything.

The 3d view item "Extra information" is HORRIBLE. It wants you to land on one completely random arbitrary spot within a sphere with like a 5 degree or less of precision, and then the information it gives you is really dumb and not at all needed for the game.

The combat feels really clunky. The combat in the previous games feels smooth, but in this one something is just off. I feel that the game wants me to always play super stealthy, but it makes it almost impossible, especially with your arrows usually not being able to 1-shot 1 or more enemies. Level design and enemy placement for fighting is not well thought out.

The game is also very arbitrary on whether or not you make jumps that you attempt. And way too often it is not even remotely clear where you are supposed to move next. I wouldn't care to count the number of times I died for BS reasons, or trying over and over to figure out what the game wants me to do.

As for the story, meh. [spoiler]I don't appreciate playing the ANTAGONIST of the game who pretends to be the protagonist. Everywhere Lara goes she causes mass death and destruction. I find myself pretty much always agreeing with the game's supposed "antagonist" over Lara.[/spoiler] And I'm not even going to go into the eye rolling Trinity silliness.

The dungeons (erm... tombs) are also kind of dumb. In all of the first game, and most of the second game, the dungeons felt like they fit into the environment. In this game dungeons are randomly strewn about with flashy but ridiculous mechanical obstacles.

In the end, I think the developers just didn't give any real thought into the game. I would bet it was done by low paid employees who were handed the project and told "just make it good and cheap enough so we can make some money off it". Don't waste your time.

[b]Preview[/b] 
Good Adventure game. Third-person camera/view. Decent story/plot. Puzzle focused, Less Gunplay, 10 to 12 hours campaign (extending up to 50 hours for full exploration, tombs, sides missions).Lack of proper boss fight. 
Excellent Graphics (with Ray Tracing). Photographer Mode.

[b]Overview[/b]
Much like its predecessor, SOTR is a good adventure game that focuses on solving puzzles. The story and the plot are decent. The puzzles in the game are hard and will test your puzzle-solving ability/skill. But one would get a feeling of satisfaction once they are able to solve the puzzles by themselves. The game is based around the adventure of the infamous archaeologist and our favourite Lara Croft. Lara have grown and have matured a lot when compared to the game’s predecessors.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The player will once again delve into the shoes of Lara Croft and will adventure around the world while solving riddles, puzzles, mysteries and discovering new places that were abandoned for hundreds of years. The game is played in “third-person view.”  Exploration and “puzzle-solving” are the core aspects of the game with elements of gunplay, stealth and archery. There is a coop mode which allows players to explore the challenge tombs together. It is not connected to the main story campaign which is “exclusively solo.” This coop mode can be accessed from the main menu, “challenge tomb sections.” 

[b]Game Duration[/b]
The game can be completed in 10-12 hours if only the main campaign/story is focused. For completeness, it can take up to 50 hours which includes collecting artefacts, documents treasures, exploring tombs etc. 

[b]Combat, Mechanics and Weapon variety[/b]
Combat is decent. If you are exclusively looking for gunplay and “heart-pumping action” then this game might not meet your expectation since it is more of an “adventure-based” game with a heavy focus on puzzle-solving and exploration. There are some gun categories in the game like assault rifles, shotguns, pistols. In addition to gunfights, Lara can use her bow and arrow as well.  The player can craft/buy modified ammos like “explosive shells” for shotguns, “flare rounds for pistols”, fire arrows/fear arrows for the bow etc. Stealth mechanics and stealth kills can also be used in certain combat situations. Some stealth kill/mechanics include 

~“Hiding in bushes” and then assassinating the enemy when they passed by an unnoticed Lara; 
~“Climbing over trees” and using ropes to hang/tie up the enemy and pull up.
~Hiding underwater and dragging the enemy underwater for a quick kill.

These are some cool mechanics that the player will enjoy. Some other mechanics include “targeting multiple targets at once and releasing volleys of arrows”, slowing of time while aiming guns/arrows and some other mechanics. Overall I would say the combat is decent and enjoyable although it may not satisfy some hardcore gamers who exclusive love action/gunplay.

[b]Enemy Type[/b]
Enemies ranges from human enemies like military, gangsters, local thugs, tribes to wild animals like jackal’s, jaguars, wolfs etc.  Compared to the human enemies, the animals are more challenging to defeat.

[b]Game Difficulty[/b]
 The game has four difficulty settings which can match all category of players ranging from casual players to hardcore players. In addition to combat/action difficulty there are separate difficulty setting for exploration, puzzles. You can set the “action/combat” difficulty to the hardest while keeping the “puzzle difficulty” to lowest. “Lower puzzle difficulty” highlights some hints/objects which the players need to interact during a sequence/section of a puzzle.

[b]Graphics[/b]
Excellent and Gorgeous. Have Ray tracing feature as well. A “photographer mode” is available which allows the player to take screenshots while in-game. The player can say/adjust the picture colour, brightness, saturation, hues and some other aspects while taking the screenshots. Even on lower-end specs, the screenshots could look gorgeous and beautiful if correct adjustments are made while taking the screenshots.

[b]Sound and Music[/b]
It is good and matches the game situation. Voice acting is also good and it brings life to the characters.

[b]Exploration, Puzzles, Crafting, Skill Path[/b]
“Exploration” is the heart of this game. The players are encouraged to explore as much as they can to discover hidden mysteries, documents, artefacts which could craft a story of their own if all the ones in their particular series are collected. The challenge tombs in the game offer some tough puzzle which the players need to solve. There are around 16 challenge tombs (9 main games, 7 DLC) in the game. It is not mandatory to complete the tombs. Although it is recommended that the player complete the tombs as completing them offers excellent rewards which range from equipment’s, skill points, special skills, weapons. 
 The player can craft special arrows like fire arrows, fear arrows which have special effects when used. For instance, a fear arrow will cause fear among an enemy who is being shot and that enemy will shoot anyone in their sight including their own ally. The players can also craft bombs, smoke grenades, flares, medicinal recipes, some status alteration mixtures.   The “status alteration mixtures” can be crafted from herbs, special plants that can be gathered throughout the world. “Status alteration” includes enhancement of Lara’s vision, endurance, slowing time, instant healing and some others.
Lara can use a variety of skills which can help her in combat, stealth, any puzzles. Skills can be upgraded through skill points which are obtained by Lara by gaining experience points. Experience points can be acquired from fighting, discovering, solving the puzzle, completing missions and some other actions. Some puzzle related skill includes “revealing traps” while using focus mode while an example of stealth kill includes killing two enemies at a time who are adjacent to each other.

[b]Some flaws[/b]
The Enemy AI is not great and combats especially gunplay needs improvement.  There is no proper “boss fight” well except for the final enemy which is also too easy. At least the second hardest difficulty is required so that it can offer a challenge to the player. The player will die a lot more from “unsuccessful wall grips”, ledge grips”, “failed jumps” than getting killed in the hands of the enemy. Sometime, unable to match some puzzle sequence will instantly kill the player (by piercing arrows, fires etc.). The “puzzles” can be too hard at some places and there are quite some glitches which will force the player to reload that part/area. Fortunately, the autosave option is good which autosaves a lot making it somewhat easy to progress. 
Also, there will be some section/ mission where Lara had to switch to particular dress so that she can interact with certain groups of people. This is quite annoying since you are not sure when you need to equip Lara with the desired outfit. The outfits can only be changed in base camps (the save points in the game). If the player has not discovered the basecamp near the mission area, then chances are that they had to backtrack a lot to earlier basecamp to change the dress/outfit to progress further in the mission. Changing weapons, outfits, bows, fast travel, upgrading skill can be possible only when using basecamps. The crafting system could have been improved.

[b]Recommendation and Verdict[/b]
Despite some flaws that are mentioned, the game will offer a pleasant experience for the players who would like to sit back and relax. It is recommended that the players complete all the challenge tombs in the game which will be highly rewarding. If the thrill of “adventuring through harsh lands,” “climbing steep and dangerous mountains,” “traversing extreme climatic conditions”, enjoying the gorgeous scenery and landscape means anything to the player then this game can be enjoyed a lot.

[b]My Rating[/b] 
7.5/10

Negative review because it's not possible to give something in the middle.

The good:
- If you've played the previous two games, this is more of the same. You know what to expect.
- Stellar beginning/ending hours of the game.
- The focus on tombs is a welcome change. If you play on Hard mode with Survival Instinct turned off, finding out what to interact with in the environment/scoping out the surroundings is engaging.
- Graphics and environments are beautiful. This is one of the best-looking games I've played.
- The swimming sections are fantastic. The game is littered with them. They are the best aspect of the game.


The bad:
- The levels themselves, unlike the previous TR games, are very small and linear. There's a few large environments, but unlike the previous games, this doesn't give you the sense that if you see something, you can reach it. A lot of freedom has been removed from the player. Stages also have arbitrary barriers to block you. You may be able to walk among the plants on the left side, but for some inexplicable reason, the plants on the right of the same walkway may act as a wall. You can only double-hop on specific walls; all other walls are just barriers to keep you from progressing, so you'll often find yourself testing where the game does or doesn't let you interact to know where to go. And most cliffs you can't even fall from since the game blocks you from walking over the ledge. Previous games had an element of environmental danger/adventuring, while this game neuters that. Understandable from the point of view of streamlining and reducing bugs, as the amount of environments is massive, but if the game is now focused on the environments, doesn't removing their danger go against that design?
- The game only really lets you reach most points in just one way, with automatic platforming/climbing. It does not feel engaging at all. Popping in Rise for a few minutes, even though the platforming is also streamlined, you can feel there's an element of danger and unpredictability that was not captured in Shadow. The problem may be that the game "magnetizes" Lara so that she hovers in the air towards where you're jumping, regardless of how close or far away you were when you jumped. The previous games also had this, but in this one it feels even worse. There were innumerable places where I could not understand how the game allowed me to make a jump. It's OKAY to die from an ill-timed jump. That was the entire purpose of the old TR games. Yet this game is, again, afraid to let you die and become frustrated.
- The skill tree and the weapon upgrades are pointless. Over half the skill tree upgrades are battle-based, and the game has only a handful of combat encounters until the very end. In addition, the skills are offense-based but the gameplay is based around stealth--nearly every encounter begins with guards looking for Lara as she hides. There's a few encounters with wildlife, but they should have been random and possible at any time, instead of confined to just a few areas defined in a map.
- The craftable and collectable items. They are EVERYWHERE. New large area? Here's 15 resources for you to plunder. New small room? Here's 5 resources. Underwater death passage with eels and piranhas? Here's some pots for you to open to pull out bird feathers and jaguar skins. The most ridiculous moment of this was when I spent three minutes climbing up a mountain with a new rock-climbing skill, and you reach an absolutely inaccessible area on top that no human could have ever reached, as it's blocked off from all sides. Yet here's a small container that contains another animal felt. Or the death temple with the cultists--which is littered with baskets of fresh berries for me to heal myself. It's ridiculous, and it detracts from the game SO much to have to be constantly collecting all of this garbage. It killed the immersion.
- There is no challenge, even on Hard mode. For the previous point, the problem with the game is that it seems afraid that you may get stuck because of difficulty. It does not want you to ever run out of items to craft ammunition or healing herbs with. As such, you're always going to have 36/36 of every item, to the point where you won't even be able to pick up new items, and will have to sell off the surplus to the merchant. At which point this becomes a game about hoarding in order to buy satchels to let you hoard even more. It would have been much more refreshing if resources were limited so that you have an element of danger and strategy with the enemies--at least on Hard mode.
- The side missions in the towns. Who thought this was a good idea? That said, points for the towns and villagers feeling like something organic. A lot of care was put into designing these, and it was nice to see civilization included in a TR game. 

Final thoughts:
Shadow suffers because it pulls elements from the two previous games and tries to incorporate them to make this feel like one of the "trilogy," when in fact most of those elements are now out of place since this is no longer a combat-focused game. The game should have been more streamlined with no skill tree, no alternate weapons (just keep the new ammunition types), and no crafting. I was disappointed because I felt Rise did everything well, and this game took what Rise did without understanding why it was successful there--it just felt misguided. That said, it was still enjoyable, and this is by no means a bad game.

I'm hoping that this was the final game of its type, and that the next Tomb Raider reworks all the mechanics and keeps moving in the direction of tomb raiding and exploration. It's time to move on.

If you're considering buying this game, you probably played the first two, so you should get this one anyway, just to get the trilogy done. However, IMO, it isn't too good of a game.

Minuses: 

- I found that the main story is somewhat convoluted, has many annoying coincidences that allow the unlikely chain of events to occur. The story itself is basically a worse repeat of previous games. Lara is after a magic relic that can destroy the world, Illuminati is after it, as well, and there's some plot in between to get you from cutscene to cutscene. The quests themselves are clearly padding: "We must infiltrate this tomb and get this artifact - oh no, one of our friends got captured during the mission, spend another mission rescuing them - oh no, another person got captured while rescuing the first person, lets' rescue them, etc." They try and fail to tug at heart strings here and there by killing off people I could never get myself to care about. There is no payoff at the end. I was upset at the dumb ending. They even tried to do something interesting in the end, but then chickened out.

- I hated the boring side quests.

- There's not much personal growth to ANY of the characters. You find out Lara's, her friends', her allies, and the antagonists' goals from the start, and they do not change. No one learns anything. The antagonist dies repeating the same mantra he's been chanting all game. No part of the story made me feel sorry for anyone who died. I never connected with any character, including Lara, who is amazingly plain in her character. 

- When not in stealth, combat and combat movement are clunky and annoying. 

- Having played on the hard difficulty, I decided the entire skill tree is optional. The few combat scenarios are either easily done in plain stealth by attacking and dragging enemies into the bushes, or picking off the 5 enemies in each area with a machine gun. I think the game gave me 2 whole opportunities to use the skill for pulling an enemy up a tree. The combat arenas are much less vertical than they really must be in a Tomb Raider title. 

- Climbing sections are boring. It's always readily apparent which way to go, there's always only one way to go, and if you see a handhold, your path certainly lies through it. In addition, those sections feel extremely long.

So-So's:

+/- The tombs are numerous and interesting. On higher levels of difficulty, the game doesn't hold your hand about the solutions, and I found that despite their vast number, each was unique enough and interesting to figure out. However, their length and vast amount had me wanting to skip them toward the end, as they become too much of a distraction. The puzzles themselves challenge my suspension of disbelief, as unbelievable convoluted contraptions from eons ago are still functional, despite being wood and rope based, and Lara has to struggle through them despite the fact that the solution to most would be a 15-foot ladder. The solutions conveniently use Lara's unlikely equipment every time.

+/- Game feels long, but it feels artificially so. I finished it in 15 hours (only getting maybe over half of the many optional letters and artifacts, not 100% completion), and I couldn't wait to get to the end. Every part of it, from super long climbing sections, to mostly uninspired cutscenes between quests that they clearly put in to pad the game, to mechanical rooms with enemies, to stupid fetch side quests, seems to exist to send you on another wild goose chase to distance you from finishing the game.

Positives:

+ Graphics are mostly good to great, especially the landscapes and vistas. Faces are meh.
+ The experience can be very cinematic, with many massive events that you have to run through or escape through.

While my review seems very harsh, I will say the game is not TERRIBLE in any category. Its story, characters, quests, and mechanics are merely average to below-average.

I loved Tomb Raider and Rise of Tomb Raider and got 100% achievements on both. I believe those games had the perfect balance of exploration, combat, and story. However, in this game, there is a severe lack of combat compared to the other titles. I think this was intentional due to fans saying the other games had too much combat and too little exploration, which might be a fair criticism but the overall change killed a lot of fun for me. I remember I played a 3 hour session of this game and had a single combat fight. Most of those 3 hours was me holding "w" on the face of a rock wall or spamming my space bar trying to skip an unskippable 20 minute long cut scene with boring dialogue and characters I did not care about. 
I love exploration, puzzles, and a good story. But I want a balanced amount of all that and combat, especially because the reward for exploration and puzzles makes you more effective in combat. Doing a difficult puzzle in a challenge tomb increased your combat performance and could give really unique options to your play style. If you reward players for the exploration and puzzle solving by making them stronger fighting enemies, it is really only a reward if there are enemies to fight in the first place. For example, one tomb I completed gave me a "take less damage from melee attacks" piece of clothing. And my first thought was melee attacks were not an issue for me at that moment, the real issue was a lack of melee attacks. 

It's also strange how developed the combat system is for such a few amount of encounters. There's an extensive skill tree with interesting and creative choices to craft your own unique style. A fully fleshed out crafting system with a large amount of weapons and modifications to choose from. Almost a hundred different outfits and costume combinations that provide unique bonuses to Laura. All of which rely on exploration and tomb raiding to acquire. But once you have these fancy gadgets, weapons, skills, and clothes, what do you even do with them? 

If you played the first 2 games (of the new series) and thought there was too much combat, you are going to love this game. The story starts off really good, picking up where Rise left off, the graphics in its lush environments are beautiful exploration is the best the series has to offer. The tombs are hands down the best in the series as well also has a lot of time and attention to detail in its puzzles. And while it can be tedious to go back and collect what you missed, there is so much variation in its environments It didn't bother me too much. Especially with difficult options for puzzles, exploration, and combat its nice to have some of these more challenging puzzles have some hints if you are struggling.

Its combat is a ton of fun with a lot of new things added, like fear arrows to make enemies commit friendly fire before dying. The mud camouflage to blend with the environment, climbing up trees and either do an aerial takedown or use rope arrows to hang them from the tree. More guns to get with various upgrades, with gold to purchase things like ammo pouches, increases, and attachments, though the shotgun is pretty underwhelming. However, as people have said, there isn't a lot of combat throughout the game compared to the first one, which is a shame. It's a waste to use your skill points for combat early in the game, as it’s better used for other skills. It's also really frustrating that enemies don’t respawn in an area you revisit to add some additional combat, and worst of all, unlike Rise, there is no level selector or combat mode, so if you want to fight some more, you have to replay the entire game over. All of these cool mechanics, like the mud stealth that took a lot of time and effort to create and playtest is barely used in comparison to what you will be doing in the game. The final boss was one of the most boring and underwhelming I have experienced in a long time. Yeah, the arenas look cool, but it boils down to run and gun dodging his attacks and shoot enough times to melee him rinse and repeat like 5 times, and that's it. 

Also, the game is way too easy on hard. I get that there is a harder mode above that, but it's only available on New Game Plus, and most people won’t do that, so it makes the game kinda easy, especially when you carry so many healing berries by the end. Because of this, the other things like using other berries to increase the slow down aim time or perception vision all feel pointless as i never actually used them, unless you want to 100% everything, the game is easy enough to navigate as it is.

Initially, it was fine as Laura believed they had the box, but once she realized they didn’t have it that should have been the moment to move on. But no she stays and helps people with their mundane problems, as they exposition dump the tribe’s culture. It would have been fine, but the writing isn't very good as it gets boring and confusing as they mix people, places, and concepts, some you get to see in the game, and other things you don’t. In the context of how this game starts, I don’t care because I wasn’t made to care, as all we are after is the box. They throw a curveball that the villain is somehow closely connected with Paititi, and Trinity controls them. This felt like this connection was thrown together at the last minute in an attempt to make this part of the game make sense. The flashbacks of Laura as a kid were a nice touch. Also, they did my boy Jonah so dirty in this one; they get split up a lot and always seem to make it to where I take the long, dangerous path. It isn't until the last quarter of the game that he does anything to help Laura at all. And that ending, nothing makes sense, nothing is explained, nothing feels like it connects from the story prior, and you are left confused by the end as the credits roll. The good news is...this is almost exactly the same game as the very excellent Rise of the Tomb Raider. The bad news is...this is almost exactly the same game as the very excellent Rise of the Tomb Raider.

   I'll admit to being the teeniest, tiniest bit disappointed that, yet again, we're more in the territory of sneaking-and-killing humans, and tussling with very natural wildlife, than we are in the realm of encountering more exotic fauna like T-Rexes, centaurs and mummified cats. This is still very much the modern, gritty, rebooted Tomb Raider; and while I'm generally adoring the series, I'm not sure I'm lusting after another one beyond this unless they change things up a bit more. (Christopher Nolan only made three of his modern, gritty, rebooted Batman films after all.)

   None of which is to say that there isn't a smidgen of newness. The flashback in which you play a pre-teen Lara was especially novel, and this and other aspects of the game certainly aspired to filling in a bit of our heroine's backstory. Such characterisation will always be welcome in [i]my[/i] world. (Even if some of this good work is partly undone by Lara's recent transformation into a human being of unbelievably altruistic proportions. Don't worry, though, she's still as much of a kleptomaniac as she always was, and seems to feel no shame whatsoever about stealing left, right and centre from the very people she is so selflessly trying to help!)

   There's also a bit more puzzle-solving than previously, though we're still not back in the realms of the earliest Tomb Raider games (and thank feck for that, considering how crap I am at puzzles)! And there's a wee bit more actual "tomb-raiding", as promised in the game's promo, as well as a good deal more swimming (and some additional danger in the water itself). Finally, there's a few new minor mechanics - especially in the stealth department - but nothing terribly groundbreaking or game-changing.

   A good 95% of the playtime will, in any case, seem quite familiar to anyone who conquered the last two games. Again: not a bad thing by a long, long stretch, but also not a reason to make another eight games in almost precisely the same vein. "So what's [i]your[/i] recommendation for the next one, then, Mr Smarty-Pants?" Well...since we've now been gifted with a very excellent trilogy about the "birth" of the Tomb Raider, how about we get on with more of that actual [i]raiding[/i]? 

   I recommend a game like the very, very first - way back in 1996! - in which we see barely a shaft of sunlight; a return to the spooky, isolated roots of the series. More monsters, more traps...and, yes, more puzzles I suppose (not [i]too[/i] hard, though)! And less human companions. Nothing against Jonah - he seems like a nice enough guy - but Lara might have to brave the next one alone, methinks. This third entry in the current franchise certainly takes more steps in this direction than the previous two, but it's time for future devs to take the full plunge, methinks.

   A thoroughly awesome trilogy, which virtually every gamer on the planet should play through at least once. But all good things must come to an end. Here's to the [i]next[/i] trilogy in the Tomb Raider legacy, eh?

   Verdict: 9.5/10.

Shadow of the Tomb Raider is an exhilarating and unforgettable experience that captures the very essence of what the franchise has always promised - adventure, exploration, and awe-inspiring discovery. 

From the moment you start, you’re thrown into a thrilling world of climbing, crawling, diving, shooting, stealthily sneaking around, zip-lining through canopies, and hunting in dense, atmospheric jungles.

The story is compelling and mature, with fantastic performances across the board. Visually, the game is breathtaking, intricate jungle environments teeming with life and secrets, beautifully lit tombs, and jaw-dropping set pieces that are a joy to explore.

What truly stands out is the game’s commitment to exploration. More so than its two predecessors, Shadow of the Tomb Raider embraces its roots, focusing heavily on platforming, puzzle-solving, and uncovering the ancient mysteries hidden in forgotten tombs. It feels like a love letter to long-time fans, truly living up to the "Tomb Raider" name.

The jungle setting is rich and immersive, but there’s a lingering hope this won’t be Lara’s last outing. A shift to a city-based environment, perhaps a gritty, atmospheric take set in London, could be a refreshing evolution, maybe even a modern reimagining of Angel of Darkness done right.

In short, Shadow of the Tomb Raider is an exceptional game packed with memorable moments and heart-pounding adventure. It’s a fitting chapter in Lara’s journey and a must-play for any action-adventure fan.

When Tomb Raider – featuring Lara Croft was released for the PlayStation in November 1996, I was 14 years old at the time, more precisely 14 years, 11 months, 4 weeks and 1 day. I had pre-ordered the game beforehand, partly because it was meant to be the very first birthday present I would give to myself. Through video game magazines, a demo and even a TV feature covering E3 in Los Angeles, I became aware of Tomb Raider and was incredibly hyped about it. I still remember how excited and full of anticipation I was when I rushed into the store, and what an overwhelming feeling it was to take the CD-ROM out of its case, almost as if I had just discovered an ancient treasure in a Peruvian cave myself.
I would give anything today to watch my younger self playing it back then, sitting completely captivated in front of the screen, mouth wide open, while everything else around me ceased to exist. The only thing that mattered was guiding Lara from the caverns to the city of Vilcabamba, and from the lost valley to the tomb of Qualopec. It was one of the first games to offer 3D environments of significant size and complexity, the puzzles were challenging, yet still relatively fair.
Over the years, Lara Croft became a true pop culture icon, many more games followed, as well as films of varying quality, comics and unfortunately a fair amount of sexualized nonsense, until the 2013 reboot came along.

Originally, I had made it a rule for myself not to replay any game on Steam that I had already played on a console. However, since I had never played Rise and Shadow of the Tomb Raider and some incredibly cheap bundle deals came my way, I decided to make an exception. I also deliberately chose not to write reviews for the Tomb Raider games from 2013 and 2016 and because Guardian of Light and Temple of Osiris never really interested me, I skipped those entirely.
Speaking of deals, since Legend and Underworld were recently available for less than a single euro/dollar, I grabbed those as well, and I will play them along with the remastered parts 1 - 6 once a new Tomb Raider game is on his way.
So, in the further course of this review, I’ll focus particularly on aspects that struck me as truly worthy of the franchise and the Tomb Raider legacy, but also on points that were disappointing to downright disastrous, serving at the same time as a kind of warning to the developers.

When I first saw the new Lara back then, I wasn’t really surprised by her appearance. I was well aware that publisher Eidos had been dissatisfied after Underworld and that Square Enix had trademarked “A Survivor is Born.” Lara was meant to be portrayed as deeper and more vulnerable, with more character development in a cinematic sense, which by and large, they actually managed to pull off. So my first thought was: “Yea, this is indeed a more realistic version of Lara Croft.”
It also didn’t surprise me that the following titles were named Rise and Shadow of the Tomb Raider, since this seemed inspired by certain blockbuster films like Batman Begins or Rise of the Planet of the Apes, clearly aiming to compete in that same league. In Shadow, there’s a sequence that strongly reminded me of some pretty intense movies, they either copied it really well or it was served as a subtle tribute but either way, it worked brilliantly. I literally jumped up from my chair cheering, wanting more of it. I also really enjoyed the new kill variations and mechanics, and I’ll always appreciate the addition of a photo mode. As for the look and the environments, it has to be said they are undeniably impressive, and exploring the jungles of Peru because of that was a lot of fun.

Certain influences to the original, like Prince of Persia and Indiana Jones, are still clearly recognizable today. Whether it was the right decision to turn a South American character named Laura Cruz into an Englishwoman who would eventually become the Lara Croft we know is another discussion entirely. Among other things, inspired by Tank Girl, the main focus at the time was to create a female, comic-style badass character. And that’s where my first criticism begins. I’m not saying that our new Lara isn’t badass, but given the decision to portray everything in a more realistic way, I would have wished that Lara from the first reboot-game all the way to Shadow of the Tomb Raider, looked a bit more defined and athletic, though not to an exaggerated degree. In the photo mode you can actually adjust Lara’s muscle tone, and at its higher setting it gets closer to what I mean: someone who climbs, jumps and fights the way Lara does should look at least somewhat like it. Still, I can somehow live with how it is.
Where I can’t look past things however, is what follows next. In the newer Tomb Raider games and especially in this one, there are countless logical inconsistencies or outright unbelievable moments. To say countless is almost an understatement, the game is absolutely full of them, to the point where halfway through it really started to annoy me. If we’re being honest, the story and the writing are weak at best, or full of holes. That’s not something I want to experience again in a modern Tomb Raider. On top of that, there’s far too much to collect and farm, way too much unnecessary text, and an overload of weapons and upgrade options, all of which had little to none impact. The balance simply isn’t there. Then come the technical problems: icons on the map often remain even after completing the task, the objective/focus marker is sometimes inaccurate, spoken dialogue suddenly drops in volume compared to the previous cutscene, and half of my deaths weren’t even my fault. Another thing that bothered me was how the game forces you to wear specific outfits for large portions of it. Like I said before, this is not something I want to go through again. A Tomb Raider game of today that aims to impress cinematically must deliver not just action and striking visuals, but also credibility and narrative coherence.

In spite of everything mentioned above, I’m still giving Shadow of the Tomb Raider a thumbs up because beneath the uneven writing and technical issues lies an adventure worth experiencing, one that delivers atmosphere and exploration reminding me why this franchise has endured for decades.

[h1]Shadow of the Tomb Raider[/h1]

[i]"We keep the sun, but you remove the shadow."[/i]

[h1]Plot[/h1]
[i]As Lara Croft races to save the world from a Maya apocalypse, she must become the Tomb Raider she is destined to be.[/i]

[i]Shadow of the Tomb Raider[/i] (SOTR) is the conclusion to Lara Croft’s origin trilogy that started with [i]Tomb Raider[/i] followed by [i]Rise of the Tomb Raider[/i]. SOTR takes place shortly after [i]Rise of the Tomb Raider[/i] and continues the narrative following the paramilitary organization Trinity. [b]The setting has Lara venturing through tropical regions of the Americas with a strong narrative focus on Aztec, Incan, and Mayan mythologies.[/b] Each game in the trilogy has a distinct feel with the setting and SOTR continues that trend. I really enjoyed SOTR’s story; it is a dark and gritty portrayal of Lara and her mission.     
  
[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
[b]The gameplay in SOTR is phenomenal. SOTR is a notable departure from emphasizing combat encounters (they are still here) and instead strongly focuses on puzzles and exploration. [/b] It could be argued that SOTR “feels” much the same as the previous two installments but sometimes change isn’t the answer. The gunplay just still feels so satisfying. I feel that SOTR is the vision of the origin trilogy fully realized. The first two games admittedly featured very little actual “tomb raiding”, but SOTR’s tombs are perhaps it’s strongest feature. There are a ton of tombs, especially combined with the DLC, and each one feels distinct and intriguing. First runs on some of the tombs can legitimately take hours. SOTR has a number of villages that serve as central hubs to the various areas. I found myself so immersed in the exploration of it all. In addition, there are a variety of side quests that can be completed. The jungle setting, amidst all the history, is a fresh departure from the previous games. There are many artifacts and documents to uncover along Lara’s journey that give satisfying information to what is going on. Resources can be quite limited, and Lara will continually have to hunt and scavenge to replenish stock. Lara also has a ton of outfits that are earned and crafted that provide various benefits.

I enjoy a good challenge and attempting Deadly Obsession difficulty on a fresh game offered that. Deadly Obsession removes nearly all checkpoints which really adds tension, fear, and thought into every one of your actions. The difficulty is extremely adjustable; everyone will find the experience they are looking for.     

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
[b]The graphics are simply breathtaking. I found myself having to stop and take screen shots so often with the built-in photo mode. [/b] Similar to previous installments, SOTR is incredibly optimized. My build had no issue getting 60 frames per second locked at 4K resolution with only a few settings turned down. The Nvidia optimization guide shows that most settings have very minimal frame impact from lowest to highest. I want to add the weapon and outfit design are incredible. Lara’s hair, a work in progress since [i]Tomb Raider[/i], has really achieved an impressive level of detail at this point. 

[h1]Audio[/h1]
The original score was composed by Brian D'Oliveira. Such a great soundtrack. The soundtrack can be found through SOTR’s launcher with purchase of the definitive edition. There are 17 tracks and are encoded in lossy MP3. D'Oliveira has experience with South American instruments and worked with native musicians to capture the right sound for the various locations. [b]I want to add that SOTR features an immersive language audio setting which has NPCs speaking in their native language. I adored this setting.[/b] There are some inconsistencies with some main characters speaking English but it’s not out of the realm of possibility that some learned the language. All-in-all, I appreciate the effort that went into something like this and hope to see it more often.  

[h1]Bonus Features[/h1]
The definitive edition contains the complete experience: 7 challenge tombs with narrative side missions, 7 weapons, 7 outfits, 7 skills, original soundtrack, 3 outfit and weapon packs, and a fitness outfit. The challenge tombs are seamlessly woven into the game. The narrative and rewards truly make them worth playing. Every tomb in SOTR can be played in a separate score attack and time attack mode with some of them being co-op. I did them mostly for achievements but found they were really enjoyable. I could see some players really striving for high scores and low times. Completing the hardest content truly feels rewarding and the items you get are awesome. There is also a new game plus mode to carry over everything into a new game. For each new game plus you can choose mastery among the three skill trees and acquire new skills, outfits, and weapons. It is pretty awesome that SOTR incentives continued clears like that. [b]For any achievement hunters it took me around 80 hours to get every achievement. It can take way less time if you start on a lower difficulty, getting 100% completion, then begin Deadly Obsession on new game plus while purely focusing on story.[/b]

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]
[b]If you are a fan of action-adventure games with open worlds, puzzles, and combat then I fully recommend SOTR[/b]. SOTR is a much darker game than the previous installments and is a thrilling conclusion to the origin trilogy. I do recommend playing [i]Tomb Raider[/i] and [i]Rise of the Tomb Raider[/i] first but don’t think it would hinder your experience if you are just looking to hop in. Honestly, I am left with a feeling of desperation, truly hoping that they continue this series beyond Lara’s origins.

Shadows and the TR Reboot could of been something really special. It had endless potential and TR2013 was a surprise hit. But, with every game they release it seemed to get worse and Eidos was comfortable with just making mediocre gameplay decisions that don't add much value or even attempting to shake things up. Shadows ends up being extremely safe, and therefor extremely boring and formulaic. Just like Rise. 

It's like theyre trying to capture that same magic from Uncharted but not really getting it. There's no real likeable characters. No great script. Lara lacks charisma or even likeability. And, again, with TR2013 they had great potential. Lara dialogue with her mentor was memorable.

"I had to kill him."
"I'm sorry, Lara. I'm sure that was hard for you."
"It's actually surprising how easy it was."

You watch Lara grow into the Tomb Raider role and it was excellent. But, just like Rise, there's no real chemistry inbetween the cast. Jonah serves as the 'what's this?' guy so Lara can exposition dump. And to compensate, Eidos tried to TR unique by adding in 'survival' mechanics, but they're pretty inconsequential. 

I just dont get how they keep this idea that you can have a 'survival game' also be a theme park game. All you do is hold W and things explode, animals leap and roar at you, and monsters chase you around. There's no sense of urgency. No feeling of choice and consequence. The systems that are included are included to just be 'enough'. You 'can' craft, but its just inconsequential things. Smoke bombs from vials, needless upgrades for your weapons. Eidos doesn't really understand what makes a crafting system exciting. Running around collecting 5 scraps to increase the fire rate of my assault rifle by 2 isn't really meaningful crafting when your assault rifle already fires fast and tap firing is usually king. And, 9/10 you're still going to use your bow.


Eidos doesn't understand that with survival like games, crafting and surviving against the odds go hand in hand. Again, choice and consequence. I love Fallout 4's Survival Mode even with it's faults. Because it offers an environment where each decision I make leads into a consequence I have to deal with later to survive. I need to heal up, but all I have is dirty water. I could heal, and drink but I could catch a disease and I don't have any medication.  They could of been more focused on survival to really feel it and make this a unique experience. Hunger and thirst systems, fatigue systems and stamina. Mud making lara always harder to detect, but increases your chances at sickness/infections. I have literally no reason to hunt animals, but this game really thinks it's cool and wants me to. But why? For crafting materials thats in abundance?  They tip-toe around survival and just use it as an extra prompt for things like doing mud camo to go against walls. When mud walls are like mostly just for scripted events, and outside of that literally any wall would do the same. It's just like 'added flavor' that doesnt really matter. 

TR2013 also showed the reboot was looking to be pretty raw and gritty. Lara had some messed up death scenes from traps, she's stabbing people in the neck and taking them down hard. But, Eidos never really continued on with it's possible darker themes besides what's already known. 

The Tombs and puzzles in this trilogy is alright, though. Shadows still features some nonsensical stuff like Young Lara going through that whole debacle to find an old room with her mom's stuff in it. Like who sets up all this bullcrap to hide a memento room? My dude. Locks exists. Lock the door.

This series just suffers way too much from feeling extremely arcade-y and doesn't know how to handle it's new identity. Survival but Lara is the luckiest girl in the world. Trapped in a cavern, she rounds the corner and finds climbing boots that perfectly fit her feet. Kill a dude, and his gun disappears. Why? Why are they so focused on Metroidvania progression and scripted scenes? They lock the shotgun to progression regardless of what the enemy has because it was vital to a scripted scene where Lara discovers it and they can show shotguns open up barricaded doors. Which also makes no sense because why would it be shotgun exclusive when you've shown Lara break things down with her climbing gear?

Duno how you make three games and theyre all practically the same game. They focus so much on making Lara's face extremely detailed. I mean, tbh, it's the perfect analogy for this series. Lara's face being so extremely detailed and pretty while everyone else looks flat and expressionless. It really makes me sad as a long-time Tomb Raider fan. And, it even makes me more sad that she never gets her iconic dual pistols. Not even as an unlockable. Again, they hinted this in TR2013 but never brought it up again. I guess they figured the bow was going to be Lara's new weapon?

I hope this isn't the end to Lara Croft. I want her to return to glory. But, this ain't it. They want grand scripted scenes like the Uncharted series but lack the 'action-adventure' thrills of it. They want survival, but Eidos is too scared or unwilling to give you *actual* survival.  But, it feels as much survival and wilderness as going to the zoo and seeing the sights. I don't know how Metal Gear Solid 3 manages to feel more connected to it's environment and have  the player feel like they're out surviving against the wilderness. 

 I also noticed how TR2013 Lara's titties are much bigger than Rise/Shadows Lara because of the outfits being selectable, lol. That made me sad.

The game is quite buggy. If you happen to have the same issues, here are my fixes that I scraped from online forums: 

1. Glitches: 
If you're having trouble with glitches (like getting stuck rappelling or nothing happening when you trigger an action prompt to solve a puzzle) try changing the display to the lowest resolution and continue the game. Change it back when you're good to go.

2. Cache/Item Bugs: 
I can't emphasise this enough, MAKE SURE YOU HAVE DIFFERENT SAVES AS YOU PROGRESS THROUGHOUT THE GAME or you will have to restart, especially if you're playing for completion. If you have collected a certain item such as a cache or a document and it hasn't registered on the map, exit the game fully after saving, relaunch the game, and continue. Hopefully this should be enough to fix the registering issue. If not, you may have to go back to a previous save and try again.

3. Audio Issues: 
If you're not getting any dialogue audio or subtitles, exit the game to the main menu after saving. Change the audio and subtitle language to any other language and continue the game. Once the audio/subtitles are back, switch back to your language of choice.

I really wanted to like [i]Shadow of the Tomb Raider[/i] ([i]Shadow[/i]) more than I did. The idea of going back to the series' roots with more tombs, puzzles, and exploration sounded great, and to be fair, those parts are pretty good. The problem is there are just too many of them and not enough of anything else. The platforming feels great, the environments are gorgeous, and some of the tombs are genuinely fun to figure out. But somewhere along the way, the game forgot that I might want to do something besides climb walls and solve puzzles for hours on end. I thought [i]Rise of the Tomb Raider[/i] had pacing issues, but [i]Shadow [/i]somehow overcorrects in the opposite direction. By the end, I was more ready for the game to be over than I was excited to see what came next.

[b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] The tombs are probably the best part of the game. They're bigger and more involved than before, with puzzles that actually make you stop and think. Figuring out how to operate some ancient mechanism or work your way through a temple feels satisfying, and the atmosphere makes these places feel old and forgotten.

[*] The game is beautiful. The jungles, ruined cities, crypts, and mountains all look fantastic, and the lighting really sells the atmosphere. It's the sort of game where I'll stop to look around simply because the scenery is nice. Visually, I really don't have much to complain about.

[*] Traversal feels great. Climbing, swinging, rappelling, and scrambling across walls are all smooth and responsive. Moving through the environment is easily one of the game's most enjoyable features. Lara has a pretty impressive collection of tools by this point, and using them to get around feels natural.

[*] I appreciate being able to adjust the difficulty for combat, puzzles, and exploration separately. Not everyone wants the same experience, and this is a useful feature. You can make the puzzles harder while keeping combat manageable, or do the opposite if that's more your thing.

[*] Stealth has some good moments. Lara can use mud for camouflage, hide in vegetation, pull enemies away from groups, and make use of environmental traps. These sections can be pretty satisfying when the game gives you room to experiment instead of just funneling you toward the next objective.
[/list]

[b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Where is all the combat?! I get wanting to emphasize exploration, but [i]Shadow [/i]goes way too far. After the opening section, there's a surprisingly long stretch where you're barely fighting anyone. By the time the game finally gives you more substantial combat encounters, it feels like it's remembered halfway through development that this is supposed to be an action-adventure game. 

[*] All that exploration gets old when there's so little to break it up. I like tombs. I like puzzles. I like climbing around ancient ruins. But even things I enjoy can become tedious when they're practically all I'm doing. The game keeps throwing more traversal and puzzle sections at me, and eventually I just wanted something different. There's a difference between focusing on a series' strengths and relying on them so much that they stop being fun.

[*] The skill tree feels pointless when so much of it revolves around combat. There are upgrades for ammunition, aiming, and takedowns, but what am I supposed to do with all these skills when the game barely lets me fight anyone? It's hard to get excited about character progression when you barely use the systems you're upgrading.

[*] Crafting and gear don't feel particularly worthwhile. You can gather materials, upgrade weapons, and collect outfits, but I rarely felt like any of it made a meaningful difference. Some outfits have useful bonuses, but then the story occasionally makes you wear specific disguise outfits instead. And some of those outfits are honestly pretty ugly, which doesn't help.

[*] The story doesn't hit as hard as it wants to. This is supposed to be a major turning point for Lara, but I never found the writing as compelling as the game seemed to think it was. Some scenes are good, and the presentation is often impressive, but the characters don't get enough room to develop, and the villain never feels particularly interesting. The story wants to be this dark, personal journey while also delivering a big jungle adventure, and the two sides don't quite come together for me.
[/list]

An amazing adventure game set in beautiful Mesoamerican jungles.

Pros:

Atmosphere: The world in this game is absolutely amazing. Scenery, authentic spoken languages, and wildlife significantly add to the weight and immersion of the game.
Exploration and Puzzles: Combined with the great atmosphere, collecting all sorts of artifacts while running around the map feels relaxing and not tedious at all. The hidden puzzle areas are much better thought-out and harder this time around. You might get stuck in certain tombs trying to figure out how to pass through for almost an hour.
Stealth: An upgraded stealth system compared to previous games. Taking down enemies this way is much more engaging than facing them in a mindless shootout.
Lara's ass: just take a look at it 

Cons:

Story: The plot is alright, though not as interesting as those in previous games. The final boss section feels a bit disappointing, as you'd expect something tremendous after being told the bad guy is trying to acquire Kukulkan's powers.
Difficulty: I did not find the "One with the Jungle" difficulty particularly hard. Limited survival instincts don't make progression much more complicated and can easily be compensated for by buying perks early on. Resources were not as scarce as expected; I even had to upgrade guns I wasn't using just to clear out my inventory. If you want a real challenge, I'd suggest playing at maximum difficulty.
Combat: As you play, you'll find yourself breezing through enemies with ease. Aim assist on the bow, perception potions, infinite rolling, and jumping make fights feel repetitive and boring. Over the entirety of my playthrough, I only died in combat a few times.
Bugs: The first bugs appear right at the beginning of the game: glitchy ropes, Lara's hair shaking wildly, and invisible body textures. At one point, certain game elements stopped working as intended if set to high graphics settings.

Verdict:
While it probably doesn't have the most compelling storyline in the series, the exploration and atmosphere easily make up for its flaws. Play it on a higher difficulty, and you'll really enjoy it.
